cases.title: Extra contract teachers in Andhra Pradesh government primary schools
cases.period: 2005-06 and 2006-07 school years (baseline June-July 2005)
cases.intervention: The Government of Andhra Pradesh authorised 100 randomly chosen rural primary schools to hire one extra contract teacher on top of their usual staff, using the normal hiring process. Contract teachers were locally hired, not professionally trained, on fixed-term renewable contracts and paid far less than civil-service teachers.
cases.verdict_basis: After two years, combined maths and language scores were 0.156 SD higher in the schools with an extra contract teacher (SE 0.045, significant at 1%), with maths 0.158 and language 0.153.
cases.design_detail: Lottery at school level: of 500 sampled schools, 100 were assigned to the extra contract teacher and 100 to the comparison group; analysis uses these 200 schools, with mandal fixed effects, lagged test scores and standard errors clustered by school. The comparison with regular teachers uses non-experimental panel data from control schools.
cases.sample: 200 government rural primary schools (100 treatment, 100 comparison) drawn from a representative 500-school sample; the two-year combined regression has 26,142 test observations (student-subject). Number of students not reported in the source.

effects.outcome: Math test score, after 2 years
effects.result: +0.158 SD (text rounds to 0.16)
effects.quote: significantly better than those in comparison schools by 0.16 and 0.15 standard deviations (σ) in math and language tests respectively
effects.page_or_section: Introduction and Table 3 Panel B, NBER WP 19440

effects.outcome: Language (Telugu) test score, after 2 years
effects.result: +0.153 SD (text rounds to 0.15)
effects.quote: significantly better than those in comparison schools by 0.16 and 0.15 standard deviations (σ) in math and language tests respectively

effects.outcome: Combined math and language, after 1 year and after 2 years
effects.result: About 0.10 SD after one year and 0.16 SD after two years
effects.quote: students in program schools scored 0.10σ and 0.16σ higher than those in comparison schools at the end of one and two years

effects.outcome: Cost comparison: salary
effects.result: contract teacher about Rs 1,000 to 1,500 per month against a regular teacher average over Rs 8,000 per month (Table 1: Rs 8,698)
effects.quote: Their typical salary of around Rs. 1000 - 1500/month is less than one fifth of the average salary of regular government teachers.

effects.outcome: Cost-effectiveness: reducing pupil-teacher ratio (PTR) by 10%
effects.result: contract teacher +0.03 SD per year; regular civil-service teacher +0.02 SD per year (regular estimate is non-experimental)
effects.quote: reducing PTR by 10% using a contract teacher would improve mean test scores in the school, across subjects, by 0.03σ/year

effects.outcome: Teacher absence
effects.result: contract teachers 18% absent versus 27% for regular teachers
effects.quote: contract teachers were significantly less likely to be absent from school than regular teachers (18% versus 27%)

effects.outcome: Heterogeneity
effects.result: no difference by baseline score; larger gains in remote schools
effects.quote: We find no heterogeneity in impact by baseline test scores, suggesting that the gains are broadly distributed among all students.

caveats: This is the September 2013 NBER working paper, not a peer-reviewed version. An earlier draft reported different second-year figures (0.15 math, 0.13 language, per a search snippet), so quote the version cited.
The regular-teacher comparison is not randomised. It uses five years of panel data from control schools.
Results apply to rural primary schools with many first-generation learners; the authors say they may not extend beyond primary school.
The paper gives salaries, not a cost per child, so a cost per SD gained is not reported here.
Treatment effects are for the school as a whole because the extra teacher was not assigned to a grade.

sources.citation: Muralidharan and Sundararaman (2013), Contract Teachers: Experimental Evidence from India, NBER Working Paper 19440

cases.title: Biometric smartcard payments for NREGS and pensions in Andhra Pradesh
cases.period: Randomised rollout from 2010; baseline survey August to October 2010, endline survey August to October 2012 (NREGS activity May to July 2012)
cases.intervention: The Government of Andhra Pradesh moved payments in the NREGS employment scheme and Social Security Pensions to biometrically authenticated smartcards, paid in villages by locally hired bank staff. J-PAL randomised the order in which sub-districts (mandals) were converted.
cases.verdict_basis: Payment speed and leakage, the outcomes the smartcards targeted, both improved significantly for NREGS. Mean time to collect payment fell 22 minutes (SE about 9) and survey-reported leakage fell Rs 25 per week (SE 13), which the paper puts at 12.7 percentage points, a 41% cut. Leakage in social security pensions fell 2.8 percentage points. Access to NREGS work did not fall.
cases.design_detail: Cluster randomised trial: 296 mandals in 8 districts were assigned by lottery to treatment (112), a buffer group (139) and control (45). Survey data came from treatment and control only (157 mandals). Intent-to-treat analysis; about 50% of payments were carded in treated mandals after two years.
cases.sample: 157 sub-districts (mandals) surveyed, about 19 million rural people in 8 districts; 880 gram panchayats sampled; endline survey of 8,774 households sampled, 365 confirmed as ghost households

effects.outcome: Time to collect an NREGS payment
effects.result: -22 minutes (control mean 112)
effects.quote: NREGS workers spent 22 fewer minutes collecting each payment (20 percent less than the control group)

effects.outcome: Average lag between finishing NREGS work and payment (days)
effects.result: -5.8 to -10 days (control mean 34); statutory limit is 14 days
effects.quote: collected their payments 5.8 to 10 days sooner after finishing their work (17–29 percent faster than the control mean)

effects.outcome: Variability of payment lag (absolute deviation from mandal median, days)
effects.result: Fell by 21 to 39 percent relative to the control group
effects.quote: The absolute deviation of payment delays also fell by 21–39 percent relative to the control group

effects.outcome: NREGS leakage (share of outlays not reaching beneficiaries)
effects.result: -12.7 percentage points (41% of control mean); control 30.7%, treatment 18%
effects.interval_or_se: Survey-minus-official gap -Rs 25 per week, SE 13 (Table 3, column 6)
effects.quote: we estimate a 12.7 percentage point reduction in NREGS leakage in treated areas (a 41 percent reduction relative to the control mean)

effects.outcome: Household NREGS earnings per week
effects.result: +Rs 35, 24% of control mean (Rs 146); official outlays unchanged
effects.quote: earnings per week during our endline study period increased by Rs 35, or 24 percent of the control group mean

effects.outcome: Households reporting NREGS work
effects.result: +7.1 percentage points (control mean 42%)
effects.quote: the proportion of households reporting having worked on NREGS increased by 7.1 percentage points (a 17 percent increase over the control mean of 42 percent)

effects.outcome: SSP pension leakage
effects.result: -2.8 percentage points (47% of control mean); pension received +Rs 12 (5%)
effects.quote: significant reduction in SSP leakage of 2.8 percentage points (a 47 percent reduction relative to the control mean)

caveats: Only about 50% of payments in treated mandals went through smartcards after two years, so estimates are of the programme as implemented, not full coverage.
The eight districts were not randomly chosen, although they resemble the state's other non-urban districts on main indicators.
The NREGS leakage rate needs a correction for households holding several jobcards, so the 12.7 point figure rests on extra assumptions.
The survey was run about ten weeks after the work, so recall error is possible.
The time saved on SSP collection was small and not statistically significant.
The authors report that the state nearly scrapped the project in 2013 because local officials passed on negative anecdotes.

sources.citation: Muralidharan, Niehaus and Sukhtankar (2016), Building State Capacity: Evidence from Biometric Smartcards in India, American Economic Review 106(10), 2895-2929
Muralidharan, Niehaus and Sukhtankar (2016), same article, publisher abstract page

cases.title: Teacher performance pay in Andhra Pradesh government schools
cases.period: Two school years of the programme, with independent tests at the end of each year.
cases.intervention: Teachers in rural government primary schools received bonus payments based on their students' improvement in independently administered tests, with a mean bonus of about 3% of annual pay. Bonuses were paid either to a whole school as a group or to individual teachers, at Rs. 500 for each percentage point of average gain above 5%.
cases.verdict_basis: After two years, students in incentive schools scored 0.28 standard deviations higher in maths and 0.16 higher in language, a mean of 0.22. They also scored 0.11 and 0.18 standard deviations higher in science and social studies, which carried no incentive. The incentive programmes raised scores 0.22 standard deviations against 0.08 for extra inputs of similar value.
cases.design_detail: Randomised trial across 300 government rural primary schools: 100 with group incentives, 100 with individual incentives and 100 comparison schools. A parallel randomisation gave two other sets of 100 schools an extra contract teacher or a materials grant.
cases.sample: 300 government-run rural primary schools in Andhra Pradesh, 100 in each of the group incentive, individual incentive and comparison arms.

effects.outcome: Student test scores after two years, maths and language
effects.result: 0.28 standard deviations higher in maths and 0.16 in language
effects.quote: students in incentive schools performed significantly better than those in comparison schools by 0.28 and 0.16 standard deviations (SD) in math and language tests respectively

effects.outcome: Mean test score effect after one year and two years
effects.result: 0.15 standard deviations after one year and 0.22 after two years
effects.quote: students in incentive schools scored 0.15 standard deviations (SD) higher than those in comparison schools at the end of the first year of the program, and 0.22 SD higher at the end of the second year

effects.outcome: Test scores in non-incentive subjects after two years
effects.result: 0.11 standard deviations higher in science and 0.18 in social studies
effects.quote: scoring 0.11 and 0.18 SD higher than students in control schools in science and social studies at the end of two years of the program

effects.outcome: Group versus individual incentives after two years
effects.result: 0.27 standard deviations for individual incentives and 0.16 for group incentives
effects.interval_or_se: Difference between the two nearly significant at the 10% level
effects.quote: the average treatment effect was 0.27 SD in the individual incentive schools compared to 0.16 SD in the group incentive schools

effects.outcome: Incentives compared with extra school inputs
effects.result: 0.22 standard deviations for incentives against 0.08 for extra inputs
effects.quote: students in schools receiving the input programs scored 0.08 SD higher than those in comparison schools. However, the incentive programs had a significantly larger impact on learning outcomes (0.22 versus 0.08 SD)

effects.outcome: Annual cost per school
effects.result: About Rs. 6,000 for group incentives and Rs. 10,000 for individual incentives, against Rs. 10,000 for each input programme
effects.quote: The average annual spending on each of the input treatments was Rs. 10,000/school, while the group and individual incentives programs cost roughly Rs. 6,000/school and Rs.10,000/school respectively.

caveats: The tests were set by an independent firm and cover only primary-school maths, language, science and social studies, so the results say nothing about other skills a teacher builds.
The sample is rural government schools in one state. Bonuses were small, at about 3% of annual pay, and the programme ran for two years.
Testing was paid for separately, at about Rs. 5,000 per school per round, and is not included in the incentive cost figures.

Figures come from the NBER working paper of September 2009, an author-hosted version of the paper published in the Journal of Political Economy 119(1); estimates in the published journal article may differ.

sources.citation: Muralidharan, K. and Sundararaman, V. (2011). Teacher performance pay: Experimental evidence from India. Journal of Political Economy 119(1). Version read: NBER Working Paper 15323, September 2009.

cases.title: Women's groups run by ASHAs in Jharkhand and Odisha
cases.period: Women's group meetings September 2010 to March 2013; neonatal deaths assessed January 2011 to December 2012
cases.intervention: Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHAs) ran a cycle of participatory learning and action meetings in which women's groups identified maternal and newborn health problems, chose strategies, put them into practice and assessed progress. The 152 ASHAs selected received 11 days of training from the NGO Ekjut on top of their government training, and were paid INR 200 for each meeting.
cases.verdict_basis: The trial's primary outcome was neonatal mortality. It was 30 per 1000 livebirths in intervention clusters and 44 per 1000 in control clusters, an odds ratio of 0.69 (95% CI 0.53 to 0.89), a significant reduction. Stillbirths, perinatal deaths and maternal deaths showed no significant difference.
cases.design_detail: Cluster-randomised controlled trial. Thirty clusters of about 5,000 people across five rural districts were randomly assigned 1:1, stratified by district, to women's groups or control. The data collection team was masked to allocation. One intervention cluster was excluded because data quality could not be verified after law and order problems, and the analysis was by intention to treat.
cases.sample: 30 clusters (estimated population 156,519); 7,219 births in 29 clusters during the 24-month assessment period, 3,700 in the intervention group and 3,519 in the control group.

effects.outcome: Neonatal mortality (primary outcome)
effects.result: 30 per 1000 livebirths in the intervention group against 44 per 1000 in the control group; odds ratio 0.69
effects.quote: The neonatal mortality rate during this period was 30 per 1000 livebirths in the intervention group and 44 per 1000 livebirths in the control group (odds ratio [OR] 0.69, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.89).

effects.outcome: Neonatal mortality adjusted for baseline differences
effects.result: Odds ratio 0.54
effects.quote: The effect was more pronounced when results were adjusted for baseline differences in neonatal mortality (adjusted OR 0.54, 95% CI 0.36 to 0.80).

effects.outcome: Stillbirths
effects.result: Odds ratio 1.18
effects.quote: Stillbirths1.18 (0.77 to 1.80)

caveats: The intervention team could not be masked to allocation.
One of the 15 intervention clusters was excluded from the analysis because data quality could not be checked.
Mortality at baseline differed between the groups, which is why the authors also report results adjusted for baseline.
The women's group meetings were run with extra training and supervision from a non-governmental organisation, so results under routine government supervision may differ.

sources.citation: Tripathy P, Nair N, Sinha R, et al. Effect of participatory women's groups facilitated by Accredited Social Health Activists on birth outcomes in rural eastern India: a cluster-randomised controlled trial. Lancet Glob Health 2016;4(2):e119-e128.

cases.title: Teaching at the Right Level and the Balsakhi remedial education trials
cases.period: Balsakhi trial 2001-2004 (Mumbai, Vadodara); later Teaching at the Right Level trials 2005-2014
cases.intervention: Pratham, an NGO working with government schools, sent a trained young woman from the community (a balsakhi) to teach basic literacy and numeracy to lagging third and fourth grade children, for about two hours of the four-hour school day. Later versions grouped children by learning level and were run by volunteers, by government teachers in camps, or by government teachers inside the school day.
cases.verdict_basis: The Balsakhi trial raised average scores by 0.14 SD in year one and 0.28 SD in year two, significant at 1% for total score in the pooled estimates. The wider Teaching at the Right Level record is mixed. The same method had no detectable effect when added to the regular school year in Bihar and Uttarakhand, and it worked when delivered in summer camps, with a protected hour in Haryana, or by the balsakhi pull-out model.
cases.design_detail: Balsakhi: schools in Vadodara and one ward of Mumbai were randomly assigned (stratified by language of instruction and other school characteristics) to receive a balsakhi in grade three or grade four; the untreated grade served as the comparison. Later trials randomised schools or villages to Pratham's delivery models.
cases.sample: Mumbai: 77 schools. Vadodara: 98 schools, with 25 more added in year two. The number of children is not given in the working paper text.

effects.outcome: Average test score, all children in Balsakhi schools, years 1 and 2
effects.result: +0.14 SD in year 1; +0.28 SD in year 2
effects.interval_or_se: total score estimates significant at the 1% level (standard errors not copied)
effects.quote: increased average test scores of all children in treatment schools by 0.14 standard deviations in the first year, and 0.28 in the second year

effects.outcome: Pooled estimate, difference and value added specifications
effects.result: +0.14 SD year 1; +0.27 SD year 2 (0.28 value added)
effects.quote: the impact of the program was 0.14 standard deviations overall in the first year, and 0.27 standard deviations in the second year

effects.outcome: Children in the bottom third of the initial distribution, year 2
effects.result: over +0.40 SD
effects.quote: children in the bottom third of the initial distribution gained over 0.40 standard deviations

effects.outcome: Children actually sent to the balsakhi (instrumental variables)
effects.result: about +0.6 SD in overall test score
effects.quote: they gain 0.6 standard deviations in overall test scores
effects.page_or_section: Direct and peer effects section, NBER WP 11904

effects.outcome: One year after the programme ended
effects.result: Average effect no longer significant one year after the programme ended
effects.quote: For the balsakhi program, the average effect becomes insignificant.

effects.outcome: Cost
effects.result: about USD 2.25 per child per year
effects.quote: The cost per student of the remedial education program is about $2.25 per child per year.

effects.outcome: Delivery model: materials only, or materials plus training, Bihar and Uttarakhand
effects.result: no effect
effects.quote: The materials-alone and materials-plus-training interventions had no effect in either Bihar or Uttarakhand.

effects.outcome: Delivery model: volunteers inside the school team, Uttarakhand
effects.result: no detectable impact
effects.quote: The materials-training-volunteers treatment in Uttarakhand had no detectible impact either.

effects.outcome: Delivery model: one-month summer camp run by government teachers, Bihar
effects.result: significant gains in language and math; reported as about +0.5 reading levels for children treated, not in SD
effects.quote: the camp improved reading scores by about 0.5 levels in just a few weeks

effects.outcome: Delivery model: government teachers with a protected hour and monitoring, Haryana 2012-13
effects.result: +0.2 reading levels in Hindi (400 schools, 200 treated)
effects.quote: Hindi test scores increased by 0.2 levels.

caveats: The Balsakhi figures come from the December 2005 working paper. The published Quarterly Journal of Economics paper reports 0.28 SD for the second year, as cited in NBER Working Paper 22931.
The Read India results report reading levels, not standard deviations, so they cannot be compared directly with the Balsakhi effect sizes.
The balsakhi was a pull-out programme, so class size also fell for children who stayed in class. The authors find the gains concentrated in children sent to the balsakhi.
The effect faded within a year of the programme ending for the average child.

cases.title: Just-in-time fund release for the rural employment guarantee in Bihar
cases.period: September 2012 to March 2013 (experiment); 2012 to 2015 (national roll-out)
cases.intervention: Under the rural employment guarantee scheme (MGNREGS), advance transfers to village councils (Gram Panchayats) were replaced by just-in-time release, triggered when officials entered worker details and a payment request in an electronic system. The reform also removed approval by the intermediate administrative tiers.
cases.verdict_basis: The main aim was to cut leakage of programme funds. Spending fell 24 percent over the intervention period while survey-reported participation rose 0.89 percentage points (30 percent of the control mean) and built assets were unchanged, so delivery to households held up as spending fell. Matching found 5 percent fewer ghost workers, and officials' median movable assets were 10 percent lower. Payment delays rose by 46 days in September to December 2012. After states adopted the system nationally, labour expenditure was 19 percent lower.
cases.design_detail: Blocks were randomly assigned to the reformed fund flow in 12 Bihar districts, with a one-third share of blocks treated in each district. The persistence of the effect was checked with a difference-in-differences comparison of district spending as the system was adopted in states across India between 2012 and 2015.
cases.sample: 195 blocks in 12 districts, covering about 33 million people: 69 treatment blocks (1,033 village councils) and 126 control blocks (2,034). A household survey covered 9,670 households in 390 village councils. The national comparison uses 4,253 district-years.

effects.outcome: Spending from village council accounts, September 2012 to March 2013
effects.result: 24 percent lower in treatment than in control village councils
effects.quote: Across the whole intervention period (from September 2012 to March 2013), spending was 24 percent lower.

effects.outcome: Self-reported participation in the scheme among surveyed households
effects.result: Increase of 0.89 percentage points, 30 percent of the control mean; the 95 percent interval runs from -0.5 to +61 percent of the control mean
effects.interval_or_se: Whole intervention period: 0.00892 (SE 0.00462) on a control mean of 0.0296 (Table 5, Panel A)
effects.quote: (0.89 percentage point, which is 30 percent of the control mean, with a 95 percent confidence interval expressed as fraction of the control mean of [-0.5;+61])

effects.outcome: Wages received from the scheme by surveyed households during the intervention
effects.result: No detectable change; the point estimate is positive and the 95 percent interval runs from -33 percent to +69 percent
effects.quote: During the intervention, the point estimate is positive (14), and the 95 percent confidence interval, expressed in percentages, is [-33 percent; +69 percent].

effects.outcome: Delay between work and payment, September to December 2012
effects.result: Surveyed workers in treatment blocks waited an extra 46 days, against a control average of 70 days
effects.quote: Compared to an average 70-day delay in the control during the first phase of the intervention (September to December 2012), surveyed workers in treatment blocks report waiting an extra 46 days for their payment.

effects.outcome: Ghost workers, measured by matching job cards to the 2012 Socio-Economic Caste Census
effects.result: 5 percent fewer ghost workers (unmatched beneficiaries) in treatment village councils
effects.interval_or_se: Match rate for single-name job cards up 1.90 percentage points, SE 0.00742 (Table 6, Panel A)
effects.quote: The estimates imply that the number of ghost workers (unmatched beneficiaries) declined by 5 percent in treatment GPs.

effects.outcome: Movable assets declared by block and village council officials, 2012-13
effects.result: Median movable assets 10 percent lower in treatment areas (8.8 percent with controls)
effects.quote: find a significant 10 percent decline in median movable assets (8.8 percent with control variables)

effects.outcome: Labour expenditure by district after states adopted electronic fund management (e-FMS), 2008 to 2016
effects.result: 19 percent lower where e-FMS for wage payments was in force, significant at the 1 percent level
effects.interval_or_se: Coefficient -770.4 (SE 179.6), in 100,000 rupees per district-year (Table 8, Panel A)
effects.quote: e-FMS decreased expenditures by 19 percent, and this effect is significant at the 1 percent level.

caveats: The experiment ran for seven months and was stopped early. Participation on the scheme was low (about 3 percent of households in the control group during the intervention), so the household survey estimates are noisy.
Leakage is measured indirectly, through the gap between official spending and survey reports, ghost-worker matching and officials' self-reported assets. The paper calls the asset result suggestive.

The national comparison uses district spending from the programme's public database and has no survey data on employment. The estimate becomes a 14 percent decline in both labour and material spending when district-specific trends are controlled for.
Spending in treatment and control village councils converged after the reform period ended in April 2013.
Quotes and page numbers are taken from the author-hosted manuscript (MIT Economics copy, June 2019); the article was published in 2020.

cases.title: Team goals and non-cash incentives for front-line health workers in Bihar
cases.intervention: Teams of ASHAs, anganwadi workers and auxiliary nurse midwives at a health subcentre were given seven shared coverage targets for maternal and child health, trained in teamwork and asked to recite a service pledge. Teams that met at least five of the seven targets in a quarter won small household items such as cookware, worth $20 to $30 per worker over a year, and teams that met all targets in every quarter also received a certificate from the District Magistrate.
cases.verdict_basis: Of the seven behaviours the team goals targeted, mothers' receipt of 90 iron and folic acid tablets was the only one with a significant difference in difference (7 percentage points, p=0.02). The others, including immediate breastfeeding, cord care, complementary feeding, family planning and DPT3, did not change significantly. Antenatal home visits rose by 15 percentage points (p=0.03), advice to mothers was reported more often, and health workers reported better coordination, so the scheme moved worker behaviour more than household outcomes.
cases.design_detail: Cluster randomised trial in which 76 health subcentre catchment areas were assigned to the team intervention plus the Ananya programme (38) or to Ananya alone (38), stratified by block and subcentre size. Effects were estimated by difference in difference using two independent cross-sectional surveys, before (May to June 2012) and 2.5 years after (November to December 2014), with survey logistic regression adjusted for maternal age and caste. Interaction terms were judged significant at p<0.10 and other comparisons at p<0.05.
cases.sample: Five rural blocks of Begusarai district, population about 530,000. Mothers who had delivered in the previous year were surveyed: 1,680 at baseline and 1,690 after implementation. After implementation, 285 anganwadi workers and 274 ASHAs also answered questions on teamwork.

effects.outcome: Antenatal home visits: at least two in the final trimester
effects.result: 15 percentage points increase attributable to the intervention
effects.interval_or_se: p=0.03 for the interaction term; no confidence interval reported
effects.quote: There was a 15 absolute percentage point increase in antenatal home visits attributable to the TBGI intervention (p=0.03 for the interaction term).

effects.outcome: Mothers receiving 90 iron and folic acid tablets (goal 2)
effects.result: 7 percentage points higher
effects.quote: receipt of iron-folic acid (IFA) tablets (7 PP, p=0.02)

effects.outcome: Breastfeeding within one hour of delivery (goal 3)
effects.result: 6.9 percentage points, not significant
effects.interval_or_se: p=0.31 for the difference in difference
effects.quote: Immediate breast feeding (within 1 hour of delivery) 3 1679 48.2 47.4 0.87 1687 54.2 60.3 0.19 3366 6.9 0.31

effects.outcome: Home visit within one week of delivery
effects.result: 7.6 percentage points, not significant
effects.interval_or_se: p=0.42 for the difference in difference
effects.quote: At least one home visit within 1 week of delivery 1679 11.2 9.8 0.80 1678 46.5 52.7 0.19 3357 7.6 0.42

effects.outcome: Mothers reporting advice from front-line workers on IFA, exclusive breastfeeding, cord care, complementary feeding and family planning
effects.result: Differences of 8 to 14 percentage points more mothers in intervention villages
effects.interval_or_se: p of 0.03 or lower for each of the five advice items
effects.quote: differences between the two groups of women ranged from 8 (cord care) to 14 (family planning) percentage points

effects.outcome: ASHAs attending three or more subcentre meetings in three months
effects.result: 87% in intervention villages against 75% in control
effects.quote: this frequency was significantly higher for ASHAs from intervention than control villages (87% vs 75%, p=0.02) but did not differ for AWWs (72% vs 70%)

caveats: Effects are difference in difference from two independent cross-sectional surveys. With only two time points the parallel trends assumption cannot be tested.
The authors applied no adjustment for multiple hypothesis tests, so some significant results could be chance findings.
Receipt of 90 IFA tablets fell in both arms (25.0% to 11.0% in control villages), which the authors attribute to supply problems, so the 7 point gain is a smaller fall in the intervention areas.
The intervention ran on top of the Ananya programme, which targeted the same behaviours. The effects are the added value of the team scheme and may differ if it were run alone.
Mothers in intervention villages were older and more likely to be from scheduled castes or tribes than mothers in control villages.
Coverage targets were far above the levels the surveys recorded, so the authors suggest some were unrealistic. Few workers counted colleagues from other villages as team members.
Teamwork was measured by workers' attitudes only. No data on team performance were available, and data on nurse midwives were limited.
DPT3 immunisation was mostly self-reported (95% of cases) in a low-literacy population.
Only five purposively chosen rural blocks in one district were studied.

sources.citation: Ananya Study Group and others. Effects of team-based goals and non-monetary incentives on front-line health worker performance and maternal health behaviours: a cluster randomised controlled trial in Bihar, India. BMJ Global Health, 2019, 4(4), e001146.

cases.title: Property tax reassessment in Chennai by government inspectors and private firms
cases.period: Reassessment April to June 2023; tax demand and collections for the 2023-24 tax year
cases.intervention: The Greater Chennai Corporation reassessed property tax on properties flagged as likely undervalued, using either its own tax inspectors or private surveying firms. Firms were paid either a fixed fee per property or a fixed fee plus a share of the tax increase found.
cases.verdict_basis: Reassessment raised annual tax demand by 6,080 rupees (about 84 percent) on properties reassessed by government inspectors and by 3,859 rupees (about 53 percent) on those reassessed by private firms, and both estimates are significant at the 1 percent level. Collections for 2023-24 rose 69 percent and 36 percent respectively. Private firms completed fewer reassessments than government inspectors, and the gap in revenue between the two is significant. This verdict is a judgement call: it answers whether reassessment raised revenue, and a reader asking whether outsourcing it to private firms worked would weigh the smaller private-firm effect more heavily.
cases.design_detail: Each of Chennai's 199 wards was randomly assigned to reassessment by government inspectors, by a fixed-fee private firm or by an incentive-contract private firm, stratified by city region. Within wards, 40 percent of street segments were randomly chosen for reassessment and the rest formed the control group. Effects on properties actually reassessed come from instrumental variables, using assignment as the instrument.
cases.sample: About 206,000 properties in 199 wards: the first list of treated street segments plus the control segments. The government had flagged about 280,000 properties as likely undervalued. 50 percent of wards went to fixed-fee firms, 25 percent to the incentive firm and 25 percent to government inspectors.

effects.outcome: Share of assigned properties reassessed by April 2024
effects.result: Government inspectors reassessed 47 percent of assigned properties, private firms 38 percent
effects.interval_or_se: Government 0.471 (SE 0.042), private 0.377 (SE 0.022); p-value of the difference 0.050 (Table 2, Panel A)
effects.quote: we find that the government surveyors reassessed 47 percent of the properties they had been assigned, compared to 38 percent for private firms (column 2).

effects.outcome: Annual tax demand on properties reassessed by government inspectors
effects.result: Increase of 6,080 rupees, about 84 percent
effects.interval_or_se: SE 540.06; control mean 7,218.18 rupees (Table 2, Panel B)
effects.quote: For those properties re-assessed by government workers, tax demand increases by an average of 6,080 rupees, or about 84 percent.

effects.outcome: Annual tax demand on properties reassessed by private firms
effects.result: Increase of 3,859 rupees, about 53 percent
effects.interval_or_se: SE 378.13; control mean 7,218.18 rupees (Table 2, Panel B)
effects.quote: For those properties re-assessed by private firms, tax demand increases by an average of 3,859 rupees, or about 53 percent.

effects.outcome: Tax collected in 2023-24 on reassessed properties
effects.result: Collections rose 69 percent with government inspectors and 36 percent with private firms
effects.interval_or_se: Government 3,964.66 rupees (SE 431.04), private 2,116.19 rupees (SE 230.27); control mean 5,721.16 rupees (Table 2, Panel B)
effects.quote: Tax collections increase by 69 percent when re-assessed by government surveyors, but by only 36 percent when re-assessed by private firms.

effects.outcome: Performance of fixed-fee firms against incentive-contract firms
effects.result: No statistically significant difference on properties reassessed, tax demand, collections or accuracy
effects.quote: We find no statistically significant differences in performance between fixed fee and incentive-based firms on any of the dimensions we examine.

caveats: The government halted reassessment on 3 June 2023 for political reasons, so only the first list of treated street segments was worked and effects are measured on that list.
Tax demand and collections cover one tax year and were measured in 2024, so the paper gives no evidence on how long the extra revenue lasts.

Only three firms were contracted (two fixed-fee, one incentive) after most interested firms declined to bid, so the private-firm results describe these firms. Government inspectors and firms also reached different properties, with government inspectors more likely to reassess the largest.
Effects per reassessed property are instrumental variables estimates for properties that were actually reassessed.
The cited version is an author-hosted working paper dated November 2025 and has not been published in a journal.

sources.citation: Duflo, E., Hanna, R., Olken, B.A. and Tandon, S. (2025). The Limits of Government Outsourcing: Property Tax Re-Assessments in India. Working paper, November 2025. Author-hosted version.

cases.title: Chiranjeevi Yojana, private obstetricians paid to deliver poor women in Gujarat
cases.period: Programme launched January 2006 in five districts and extended statewide by January 2007; outcomes compared for 2005 to 2008, survey in 2010
cases.intervention: Chiranjeevi Yojana is a public-private partnership in Gujarat that pays designated private health facilities to provide delivery care to poor women, intended to cover the costs of delivery for those who choose to give birth in a facility. The programme had paid providers over US$ 32 million as of 2012.
cases.verdict_basis: The programme was not associated with a statistically significant change in institutional delivery (2.42 percentage points, 95% CI -5.90 to 10.74) or in birth-related complications (6.16 percentage points, 95% CI -2.63 to 14.95). An independent state survey gave a similar null result for institutional delivery. Household spending on deliveries did not fall.
cases.design_detail: Observational difference-in-differences design using the staggered rollout: five early-implementing districts against 21 late-implementing districts, with district and year fixed effects and controls for maternal and household characteristics. Standard errors are clustered by block. Repeated on the third District Level Household and Facility Survey (DLHS-3).
cases.sample: 5,597 households with a delivery since January 2005, from a state-wide stratified three-stage cluster survey in August to September 2010. 6,484 households from DLHS-3 (2007 to 2008) for the parallel analysis.

effects.outcome: Probability of institutional delivery, own survey
effects.result: 2.42 percentage points, not statistically significant
effects.quote: was not associated with a statistically significant change in the probability of institutional delivery (2.42 percentage points; 95% CI: −5.90 to 10.74)

effects.outcome: Probability of institutional delivery, DLHS-3 data
effects.result: No statistically significant change
effects.interval_or_se: estimates more precise than the own survey
effects.quote: also confirms our findings that the programme’s implementation was not associated with a statistically significant change in institutional deliveries

effects.outcome: Birth-related complications
effects.result: 6.16 percentage points, not statistically significant
effects.quote: or of birth-related complications (6.16 percentage points; 95% CI: −2.63 to 14.95)

effects.outcome: Any delivery-related household spending
effects.result: 2.69 percentage points, not statistically significant
effects.quote: with the probability that households reported any delivery-related spending (2.69 percentage points; 95% CI: −1.10 to 6.48)

effects.outcome: Mean household expenditure for private-sector deliveries
effects.result: No fall, or very little fall, in spending
effects.quote: mean household expenditure for private-sector deliveries had either not fallen or had fallen very little

caveats: The study was not a randomised controlled evaluation, so the authors say confounding cannot be ruled out, though they report no pre-existing trend differences in an analysis of DLHS-2 data.
Outcomes rely on mothers’ recall of births up to five years earlier.
The authors say the minimum detectable effect on institutional delivery was about 5 percentage points, so smaller effects could not be excluded.

The authors report no data on neonatal or maternal deaths. Earlier evaluations of the programme reported much larger benefits, which they say did not address self-selection or the background rise in institutional births.

sources.citation: Mohanan M, Bauhoff S, La Forgia G, Babiarz KS, Singh K, Miller G. Effect of Chiranjeevi Yojana on institutional deliveries and neonatal and maternal outcomes in Gujarat, India: a difference-in-differences analysis. Bull World Health Organ 2014;92(3):187-194.

cases.title: Debt Recovery Tribunals and loan repayment
cases.period: Tribunals opened from April 1994 (first group of states) and from November 1996 (second group); repayment of loans sanctioned before June 1993
cases.intervention: The Debt Recovery Tribunals Act of 1993 let the central government set up special tribunals that follow a faster procedure to speed up banks' suits against defaulting borrowers, in place of the civil courts. Claims above Rs 1 million are eligible, and tribunals were opened state by state from 1994.
cases.verdict_basis: Loans with more than Rs 1 million overdue were 11% more likely to pay subsequent invoices within 180 days once a tribunal existed in the state (coefficient 0.11, significant at 1%), and late payers cut the time taken by 265 days. Within the same loans the gain was smaller, 0.03 and only significant at 10%. Interest rates on new loans fell by 2.2 percentage points in one specification (10% level) but not in borrower fixed-effects regressions, and loan sizes did not change.
cases.design_detail: Difference-in-differences using two sources of variation: the Rs 1 million claim threshold for tribunal eligibility, and the staggered opening of tribunals across states. Loans with more than Rs 1 million overdue are compared with loans below the threshold before and after a state's tribunal opened. Checks add narrow bands around the threshold, state-by-quarter fixed effects, and loan and borrower fixed effects. Standard errors are block bootstrapped by groups of states sharing a tribunal.
cases.sample: 798 project loans to 439 borrowers from one large private bank with a national presence, observed in 15,034 loan-quarters (loans sanctioned before 24 June 1993); 2,018 loans in the loan-size tests and 2,179 disbursements in the interest-rate tests.

effects.outcome: Probability an invoice is paid within 180 days, loans above the claim threshold after a state tribunal opened
effects.result: Loans with more than Rs 1 million overdue were 11% more likely to pay up within 180 days
effects.interval_or_se: Coefficient 0.11, SE 0.01; mean of the outcome 0.55 without a state tribunal and 0.71 with one
effects.quote: loans which had more than Rupees 1 million overdue were 11% more likely to pay up subsequent invoices within 180 days

effects.outcome: Days taken to pay among invoices not paid within 180 days
effects.result: Reduced by 265 days
effects.quote: even loans which did not pay up within 180 days, did reduce the time taken to pay by 265 days

effects.outcome: Probability an invoice is paid within 180 days, within the same loan (loan fixed effects)
effects.result: +0.03 in the full sample, +0.01 in the earlier-opening states and +0.05 in the later-opening states
effects.interval_or_se: SE 0.02, 0.03 and 0.02; significant at 10% in the full sample and at 5% in group 2 states
effects.quote: State DRT X Above 0.03* 0.01 0.05**

effects.outcome: Interest rate on loans sanctioned after a state tribunal opened
effects.result: 2.2 percentage points lower in levels, with no significant change in borrower fixed-effects regressions
effects.interval_or_se: Coefficient -2.15, SE 1.19 (10% level) in levels; -0.94, SE 1.34 with borrower fixed effects
effects.quote: the establishment of DRTs caused loans sanctioned subsequently to charge an interest rate that is 2.2 percentage points lower

effects.outcome: Log size of loans sanctioned after a state tribunal opened
effects.result: No significant change: -0.14 in levels and -0.08 with borrower fixed effects

caveats: All loan data come from a single private bank, so the results may not describe other lenders or public sector banks.

The eligibility threshold is on the amount overdue at the time of the reform, and the paper notes that loans far above it responded less, which may mean they were too far gone to respond to the threat of litigation.

The within-loan gain appears in the group 2 states, where tribunals opened from 1996 after the Supreme Court restored them, and not in the group 1 states, where the paper describes the effect as compositional.
Official data on case processing times were not available; the evidence on speed is a sample of 50 cases from the bank's law firm.
The figures and quotes come from the April 2006 Boston University working paper; the published article (American Economic Journal: Applied Economics 2009) reports revised estimates.

sources.citation: Visaria, S. (2006). Legal Reform and Loan Repayment: The Microeconomic Impact of Debt Recovery Tribunals in India. Boston University working paper, April 2006 (version used for the figures above). Published in American Economic Journal: Applied Economics 1(3): 59-81, 2009.
Visaria, S. (2009). Legal Reform and Loan Repayment: The Microeconomic Impact of Debt Recovery Tribunals in India. American Economic Journal: Applied Economics 1(3): 59-81.

cases.title: Delhi odd-even vehicle rationing
cases.period: Two pilot rounds: 1 to 15 January 2016 and 15 to 30 April 2016
cases.intervention: Between 8 am and 8 pm, privately owned cars with odd-numbered licence plates could run only on odd dates and even-numbered plates only on even dates. Women drivers and cars carrying more than two passengers were exempt, and Sundays were excluded.
cases.verdict_basis: The scheme aimed to cut traffic and air pollution. Fine particle concentrations (PM2.5) in Delhi were 13% lower than in neighbouring satellite cities during the January round, with triple-difference estimates of 32.77 and 33.45 micrograms per cubic metre at the 5 percent level in two of three specifications. There was no detectable effect in the April round. Road congestion fell in both rounds, by around 0.10 to 0.12 minutes per km (9 to 10% of average excess delay) in the pooled estimates, but 41 to 43% of drivers who stopped using their primary car switched to another private vehicle.
cases.design_detail: Air quality: difference-in-differences and triple-difference comparison of hourly PM2.5 at Delhi monitors against monitors in Faridabad, Gurgaon and Rohtak, for restricted hours on programme days against other times. Traffic: a regression discontinuity around the end of each round using Google Maps travel times on 150 routes, and a panel of drivers using the essentially random assignment of odd and even plates.
cases.sample: Air quality: hourly PM2.5 from 10 monitors (7 in Delhi, 3 in neighbouring towns) from November 2015 to April 2016, with regression samples of 3,667 observations from 8 monitors for January and 3,438 from 9 monitors for April. Traffic: 150 routes in Delhi and daily phone surveys of 556 male drivers recruited before the first round and 494 before the second.

effects.outcome: PM2.5 in Delhi relative to satellite cities, January round
effects.result: Fine particle concentrations in Delhi were 13% lower than in neighbouring cities during the January pilot.
effects.interval_or_se: Triple-difference estimates in Table 2 are -32.77 (standard error 10.37) and -33.45 (standard error 10.83) micrograms per cubic metre, both significant at 5%; the bootstrapped specification gives -37.66 (standard error 22.21), significant at 10%
effects.quote: Relative to surrounding satellite cities, fine particle concentrations in Delhi’s air were lower by 13% during the January pilot.

effects.outcome: PM2.5 in Delhi relative to satellite cities, April round
effects.result: The programme did not affect Delhi's air quality in April.
effects.interval_or_se: Triple-difference estimates in Table 2 are -1.801 (standard error 15.20), 0.635 (standard error 9.283) and -0.642 (standard error 8.920) micrograms per cubic metre
effects.quote: the program did not affect Delhi’s air quality during the warmer month of April

effects.outcome: Travel time excess delay on 150 Delhi routes, January and April rounds
effects.result: Excess delay fell by about 0.10 to 0.12 minutes per km, 9 to 10% of average excess delay.
effects.interval_or_se: January estimates -0.116 (standard error 0.018), -0.124 (0.037), -0.121 (0.037); April estimates -0.096 (0.015), -0.143 (0.032), -0.141 (0.032) minutes per km (Table 1)
effects.quote: The results point to a reduction of around 0.10-0.12 minutes/km. Given the average excess delay of 1.1-1.2 minutes/km without the policy, this effect size represents 9-10% of average excess delay.

effects.outcome: Use of the primary car by surveyed drivers, first round
effects.result: In the first round 51% of drivers used their primary car on an unrestricted day, against 18% on a restricted day.
effects.quote: during the first round of the policy 51% of drivers use their primary car on an unrestricted day, versus 18% on a restricted day

effects.outcome: Where drivers who stopped using their primary car went
effects.result: Almost half, 41 to 43%, of the drivers pushed away from their primary car switched to a different private vehicle.
effects.quote: almost half (41-43%) of the drivers who are induced away from using their primary car turn to using a different private vehicle for their commute

effects.outcome: Drivers cancelling all trips on a restricted day
effects.result: Between 8 and 10 percentage points of drivers cancelled all trips on the reference day.
effects.quote: between 8 and 10 percentage points of drivers cancel all trips during the reference day

caveats: The January air quality estimate rests on 8 monitors and 15 days. Data availability in the comparison towns was thin in January (Gurgaon 10% of hours, Rohtak 52%, Faridabad 60%).

Delhi introduced other measures at the same time, including limits on trucks and a ban on new large diesel cars. The authors argue the effect is confined to restricted hours on programme days, which points to cars, but the design cannot fully exclude these measures.
The authors report significant reductions mainly between 11 am and 2 pm, and estimates for other hours are noisy and cannot be distinguished from zero.
The January round was announced as a short pilot, so commuter behaviour may differ if a scheme runs for longer.
The traffic results measure excess delay on 150 routes and a panel of male drivers recruited at petrol pumps, not the average experience of all commuters.

Both sources are working papers. The air quality source is an EPIC-India draft file dated 2 July 2017 and the traffic source is the 11 July 2016 working paper hosted by the International Growth Centre.

sources.citation: Greenstone, M., Harish, S., Pande, R. and Sudarshan, A. (2017). Clearing the air on Delhi's odd-even program. EPIC-India working paper, draft of 2 July 2017.
Kreindler, G. (2016). Driving Delhi? Behavioural Responses to Driving Restrictions. Working paper, 11 July 2016, International Growth Centre.

cases.title: Graduation programme for the ultra-poor in West Bengal
cases.period: Multi-site trial run between 2007 and 2014. In West Bengal the first follow-up came about two years after the programme began and the second about three years after.
cases.intervention: Bandhan gave selected ultra-poor households a productive asset worth 6.53 goats at local prices, which most households used for livestock. The asset came with a consumption stipend, business training, regular home visits that included health education, and access to savings.
cases.verdict_basis: In the West Bengal sample, the per capita consumption index was 0.296 standard deviations higher in treated households two years after the start and 0.228 higher about a year after the programme ended, both significant. The asset index was 0.650 and 0.712 standard deviations higher at the two follow-ups. Across all six countries consumption rose 0.12 standard deviations, with no fall-back a year after the programme ended.
cases.design_detail: Randomised trial in which eligible households within each village were assigned to treatment or control. Effects are intention-to-treat. Only 52% of the households selected in West Bengal took up the programme, so the estimates are diluted by non-participation.
cases.sample: West Bengal site: 816 observations at the first follow-up and 879 at the second in the consumption regressions. The six-country trial (Ethiopia, Ghana, Honduras, India, Pakistan, Peru) covers 21,063 adults in 10,495 households.

effects.outcome: India (West Bengal) per capita consumption index, standardised, at two follow-ups
effects.result: 0.296 standard deviations at the first follow-up and 0.228 at the second, treatment versus control
effects.quote: Total per capita consumption, standardized 0.296*** 0.001 0.228*** 0.002

effects.outcome: India (West Bengal) total consumption per capita per month, second follow-up
effects.result: PPP US$6.18 higher in treated households

effects.outcome: India (West Bengal) asset index at two follow-ups
effects.result: 0.650 standard deviations at the first follow-up and 0.712 at the second

effects.outcome: India (West Bengal) incomes and revenues index at two follow-ups
effects.result: 0.608 standard deviations at the first follow-up and 0.666 at the second
effects.quote: Incomes and revenues index (5 components) 0.608*** 0.001 0.666*** 0.001

effects.outcome: India (West Bengal) physical health index at two follow-ups
effects.result: 0.160 standard deviations at the first follow-up, significant, and -0.017 at the second, not significant
effects.quote: Physical health index (3 components) 0.160** 0.025 -0.017 0.746

effects.outcome: Pooled across six countries: per capita consumption at the first follow-up
effects.result: 0.12 standard deviations, equal to PPP US$4.55 per capita per month. This is a pooled figure across six countries, not the India figure
effects.quote: per-capita consumption increases by 0.12 standard deviations (q-value 0.001), which is equivalent to PPP US$4.55 per capita per month

effects.outcome: Pooled across six countries: asset index at two follow-ups
effects.result: 0.26 standard deviations at the first follow-up and 0.25 at the second. This is a pooled figure across six countries
effects.quote: The asset index we construct in all countries is 0.26 standard deviations larger in endline 1 and 0.25 standard deviations larger in endline 2.

effects.outcome: India (West Bengal) benefit-cost ratio using consumption gains as the benefit
effects.result: 410%, the highest of the six sites
effects.quote: the programs all have benefits greater than their costs (ranging from 133% in Ghana to 410% in India)

effects.outcome: India (West Bengal) internal rate of return
effects.quote: They are 13.3% (Ethiopia), 6.9% (Ghana), n/a (Honduras), 23.4% (India), 9.5% (Pakistan), and 7.5% (Peru).

caveats: Half of the households selected in West Bengal did not take up the programme, so the intention-to-treat estimates understate the effect on households that took part.
Attrition in West Bengal was 17% at the first follow-up, and was not different between treatment and control.

The benefit-cost ratio and rate of return rest on assumptions about how long the consumption gains last after the third year, and on costs that were spread over the households that accepted the programme.
Figures come from the author manuscript and its supplementary tables, not the typeset journal version.

sources.citation: Banerjee, A., Duflo, E., Goldberg, N., Karlan, D., Osei, R., Parienté, W., Shapiro, J., Thuysbaert, B. and Udry, C. (2015). A multifaceted program causes lasting progress for the very poor: Evidence from six countries. Science 348(6236), 1260799. Author final manuscript with supplementary materials (MIT DSpace copy).

cases.title: Third-party environmental audits of polluting plants in Gujarat
cases.period: Audit years 2009 and 2010, with an endline pollution survey about six months after the last audit visit
cases.intervention: Treated plants were assigned an environmental auditor at random, and the auditor was paid a flat fee from a central pool rather than by the plant. A random 20 percent of each auditor's readings were checked by unannounced follow-up visits from an independent technical agency, and from the second year the auditor's pay was linked to accuracy.
cases.verdict_basis: The reform targeted truthful auditing and, through it, plant pollution. Audits in treatment plants were 81 percent less likely to falsely report compliance with the standard, and audit readings were 0.210 standard deviations higher relative to backchecks than in control plants. Average pollution at endline was 0.211 standard deviations lower in treatment plants (standard error 0.099), driven by a 0.300 standard deviation fall in water pollutants. The effect on air pollutants and on the share of readings meeting the standard (2.68 percentage points) was not significant.
cases.design_detail: Plants were randomly assigned to treatment within region, with half of the provisional sample in each arm. Reporting accuracy is measured by comparing audit readings with backcheck readings for the same pollutants and places. Pollution is measured in an independent endline survey of all plants. Standard errors are clustered at the plant level.
cases.sample: 473 audit-eligible plants in the Ahmedabad and Surat regions (233 treatment and 240 control). The endline survey collected 2,953 pollution samples from 408 plants, and the audit-report analysis uses 13,170 pollutant readings.

effects.outcome: Gap between audit report and backcheck reading (standard deviations), treatment relative to control
effects.result: Audit readings relative to backchecks were 0.210 standard deviations higher in treatment plants than in control plants.
effects.interval_or_se: Standard error 0.073 (Table V, panel C, column 1)
effects.quote: The treatment coefficient of 0.210 standard deviations (standard error of 0.073 standard deviations) indicates that auditors working in treatment plants report

effects.outcome: Readings falsely reported as below the standard, control plants
effects.result: In control plants an additional 28.8% of audit readings, relative to backchecks, were falsely reported as below the standard.
effects.interval_or_se: Standard error 0.023 (Table IV, panel B, column 1)
effects.quote: The coefficient for audit reports indicates that an additional 28.8% of readings from audits are falsely reported as below the standard.

effects.outcome: False reports of compliance with the standard, treatment relative to control
effects.result: Audits in treatment plants were 81% less likely to falsely report compliance, a coefficient of -0.234 against 0.288 in control plants.
effects.interval_or_se: Standard error 0.039 (Table IV, panel B, column 1)
effects.quote: audits in the treatment are 81% (-0.234/0.288) less likely to falsely report compliance with the standard

effects.outcome: Pollution at endline, all pollutants (standard deviations)
effects.result: Treatment plants reduced pollution by 0.211 standard deviations.
effects.interval_or_se: Standard error 0.099, significant at the 5 percent level; control mean 0.076 (Table VII, panel A, column 1)
effects.quote: On average, the treatment plants reduced pollution by a statistically significant 0.211 standard deviations.

effects.outcome: Water pollutant concentrations at endline
effects.result: Water pollutants fell by 0.300 standard deviations in treatment plants.
effects.interval_or_se: Standard error 0.159, significant at the 10 percent level (Table VII, panel A, column 2)
effects.quote: This effect is driven by a large decrease of 0.300 standard deviations in water pollutant concentrations, shown in column (2).

effects.outcome: Air pollutant concentrations at endline
effects.result: The effect on air pollutants was smaller and not statistically significant.
effects.interval_or_se: Coefficient -0.053, standard error 0.057 (Table VII, panel A, column 3)
effects.quote: The estimated effect on air pollution in column (3) is smaller and insignificant.

effects.outcome: Share of endline readings at or below the regulatory standard
effects.result: Compliance rose by 2.68 percentage points, which is not statistically significant.
effects.interval_or_se: Standard error 0.027 (Table VII, panel B, column 1)
effects.quote: compliance is estimated to have increased by a small and insignificant 2.68 percentage points.

effects.outcome: Where in the pollution distribution the reduction occurred
effects.result: The reduction sat in the right tail: point estimates fall to less than -0.5 standard deviations at the 0.95-quantile.
effects.quote: from the 0.80-quantile onwards the point estimates sharply decrease to less than -0.5 standard deviations at the 0.95-quantile

caveats: The treatment bundled four changes (random assignment, fixed pay from a central pool, backchecks and incentive pay from year two), so the effect of each part cannot be separated.
With auditor fixed effects the audit-minus-backcheck estimate is 0.153 with a standard error of 0.099, which is not significant at conventional levels.

No individual quantile coefficient in the pollution distribution is significant at conventional levels, and the mean effect is helped by a few control plants with very high readings. Top-coding the highest readings shrinks the estimate to 0.143 and 0.114 standard deviations.
Audits were submitted by 70 percent of treatment plants and 74 percent of control plants in 2009, and by 70 percent and 64 percent in 2010, so the audit-report results describe plants that submitted.
The experiment covers two industrial regions of one state and two years, and plant responses may differ if a reform is permanent.
Cited from NBER Working Paper 19259 (July 2013), the working-paper version of the Quarterly Journal of Economics article.

sources.citation: Duflo, E., Greenstone, M., Pande, R. and Ryan, N. (2013). Truth-telling by Third-party Auditors and the Response of Polluting Firms: Experimental Evidence from India. Quarterly Journal of Economics 128(4): 1499-1545. Cited version: NBER Working Paper 19259, July 2013.

cases.title: Indira Gandhi Matritva Sahyog Yojana and infant mortality
cases.period: Scheme introduced in 2011 in 52 pilot districts; births in the five years before the 2015-16 survey
cases.intervention: The Indira Gandhi Matritva Sahyog Yojana paid pregnant and lactating women a total of Rs.4000 in three instalments, in the last trimester and 3 and 6 months after delivery. Each instalment depended on health conditions such as antenatal care, vaccinations, growth monitoring and counselling sessions.
cases.verdict_basis: The programme's aim was to improve infant survival, and the study measured mortality over the first 12 months. The estimate is 1.53 fewer deaths per 1000 live births, an 8.32% fall in the infant mortality rate, with a 95% prediction interval of 1.26 to 1.80. Most of the fall came from the first four weeks of life and from the period after six months.
cases.design_detail: Matched-pair difference-in-differences using the pilot phase, in which 52 districts were chosen for the scheme by stratified random selection. The analysis used 35 treatment districts matched to 35 control districts in 24 states, with survival probabilities estimated by random survival forests on births recorded in the National Family Health Survey 2015-16.
cases.sample: 4,074 live births in treatment districts and 4,018 in control districts after dropping observations with missing data.

effects.outcome: Infant mortality, first 12 months
effects.result: 1.53 fewer deaths per 1000 live births, an 8.32% decrease in the infant mortality rate
effects.quote: IGMSY reduced the infant mortality rate by 8.32% in treatment districts, with 1.53 fewer deaths per 1000 live births [95% prediction interval: 1.26-1.80].

effects.outcome: Neonatal period, birth to 4 weeks
effects.result: 1.04 lives saved per 1000 births
effects.quote: The largest effects are observed during the first 4weeks with 1.04 lives per 1000 births saved in this neonatal period.

caveats: Child deaths in survey data are often reported with heaping at 12 months, which can bias the infant mortality rate.
Intervals are prediction intervals from random survival forests, not conventional confidence intervals.
The estimate is for being in a pilot district, whether or not a mother received the cash, so it is an intention-to-treat effect.
The study does not separate how the cash and the health conditions each contributed.
The pre-treatment check for parallel trends covers only 2010 and 2011.
The cited version is the published journal article.

sources.citation: Aizawa T. Does the conditional maternal benefit programme reduce infant mortality in India? Health Policy and Planning 2022;37(9):1138-1147.

cases.title: Immunisation camps with small incentives in rural Udaipur
cases.period: Baseline survey from June 2004 to February 2005. Endline survey from July 2006 to February 2007, about 18 months after the camps began.
cases.intervention: Seva Mandir, a non-governmental organisation, ran monthly immunisation camps at a fixed date and time in study villages. In half of those villages parents also received 1 kg of raw lentils for each immunisation and a set of metal plates when a child was fully immunised.
cases.verdict_basis: Full immunisation among children aged 1 to 3 was 6% in control villages, 18% in villages with reliable camps and 39% in villages with camps plus incentives. The relative risk against control was 3.1 for camps alone and 6.7 for camps with incentives. Most children in the best arm were still not fully immunised, so the gain is large but starts from under 2% at baseline.
cases.design_detail: Cluster randomised trial. After stratifying by administrative block, 30 villages were assigned to reliable camps, 30 to camps with incentives and 74 to control. Analysis was by intention to treat, with a neighbouring village sampled near each study village to measure spillovers.
cases.sample: 134 villages; 2,188 children aged 1 to 3 at endline from 2,898 households, including 860 in control, 379 in camp-only and 382 in camps-with-incentives villages.

effects.outcome: Share of children aged 1 to 3 fully immunised, by arm
effects.result: 39% with camps and incentives, 18% with camps only, 6% in control
effects.quote: 148/382 (mean 39%, 95% confidence interval 30% to 47%) children were completely immunised compared with 68/379 (18%, 11% to 23%) in intervention A villages and 50/860 (6%, 3% to 9%) in control villages

effects.outcome: Relative risk of full immunisation
effects.result: 3.1 for camps only versus control, 6.7 for camps with incentives versus control, 2.2 for camps with incentives versus camps only
effects.quote: 3.1 (2.0 to 4.2) for intervention A versus control, 6.7 (4.5 to 8.8) for intervention B versus control, and 2.2 for intervention B versus intervention A (1.5 to 2.8)

effects.outcome: Average cost to Seva Mandir of fully immunising one child
effects.result: $27.94 (1,102 rupees) in camps with incentives and $55.83 (2,202 rupees) in camps without
effects.quote: The average cost to Seva Mandir of fully immunising a child was $27.94 (1102 rupees, about £16 or €19) in the reliable camp with incentives and $55.83 (2202 rupees) in the reliable camp without incentives

effects.outcome: Estimated cost per fully immunised child for a government using existing health infrastructure
effects.result: $17.35 in camps with incentives and $25.18 in camps without
effects.quote: the average cost of fully immunising a child was estimated at $25.18 in camps without incentives and $17.35 in camps with incentives

effects.result: 20% near camps with incentives and 11% near camps without
effects.quote: 61/302 children (20%, 10% to 31%) were completely immunised compared with 36/265 children (11%, 5% to 16%) in villages bordering an intervention A camp

caveats: Immunisation status came partly from mothers' reports, which the authors checked against BCG scars, immunisation cards and camp logbooks.
Villagers knew which arm they were in, and may have attended camps to keep the programme running.

Baseline full immunisation was under 2%, so the gains may be smaller where coverage is already higher. The villages come from a poor, largely tribal catchment area and are not representative of Udaipur.
The trial tests reliable supply together with incentives, so it cannot separate the effect of the incentive from the effect of the camp it was attached to.

cases.title: Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illness in Faridabad, Haryana
cases.period: Implemented January 2007 to April 2010; births enrolled January 2008 to March 2010
cases.intervention: Community health workers (Anganwadi workers, accredited social health activists and auxiliary nurse midwives) were trained under the Government of India's IMNCI modules to make postnatal home visits, and physicians, nurses and community health workers were trained to treat or refer sick newborns and children. Accredited social health activists also ran women's group meetings every three months, and drug supply and supervision were strengthened.
cases.verdict_basis: Infant mortality, one of the three primary outcomes, was 15% lower in the intervention clusters (adjusted hazard ratio 0.85, 95% CI 0.77 to 0.94). Neonatal mortality over the first 28 days, the other main outcome named from the start, was 9% lower but the interval included no effect (0.91, 0.80 to 1.03). The reduction in neonatal mortality was significant only for babies born at home (0.80) and not for babies born in a health facility (1.06).
cases.design_detail: Cluster randomised trial. Nine of the 18 primary health centre areas in Faridabad district were allocated to the intervention and nine to control by a computer generated random number. Outcomes were measured by a surveillance team that was not told the allocation, using monthly household visits and follow-up at day 29 and at 3, 6, 9 and 12 months.
cases.sample: 18 clusters with a population of 1.1 million; 29,667 births in intervention clusters and 30,813 in control clusters.

effects.outcome: Infant mortality (birth to 365 days)
effects.result: Adjusted hazard ratio 0.85
effects.quote: The infant mortality rate was significantly lower in the intervention clusters than in the control clusters (adjusted hazard ratio 0.85, 95% confidence interval 0.77 to 0.94).

effects.outcome: Neonatal mortality (birth to day 28)
effects.result: Adjusted hazard ratio 0.91
effects.quote: The adjusted hazard ratio for neonatal mortality rate was 0.91 (0.80 to 1.03) in the intervention compared with the control clusters.

effects.outcome: Neonatal mortality beyond the first 24 hours (day 2 to 28)
effects.result: Adjusted hazard ratio 0.86
effects.quote: neonatal mortality rate beyond the first 24 hours was significantly lower in the intervention clusters (adjusted hazard ratio 0.86, 0.79 to 0.95)

effects.outcome: Neonatal mortality by place of birth
effects.result: Adjusted hazard ratio 0.80 for home births and 1.06 for facility births
effects.quote: in the subgroup born at home (adjusted hazard ratio 0.80, 0.68 to 0.93) but not in the subgroup born in a health facility (1.06, 0.91 to1.23)

caveats: Only 18 clusters were available, which limits statistical efficiency.

Some baseline differences remained after randomisation: the intervention areas were less accessible, had fewer births in health facilities and lower family economic status, and the analysis adjusted for them.
Mortality beyond the first 24 hours was added as a primary outcome after the first year of the study, because more than 40% of deaths occurred in the first 24 hours.
Not all newborns and families received the intervention, because it was delivered by the district health system.

sources.citation: Bhandari N, Mazumder S, Taneja S, Sommerfelt H, Strand TA. Effect of implementation of Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illness (IMNCI) programme on neonatal and infant mortality: cluster randomised controlled trial. BMJ 2012;344:e1634.

cases.title: Janani Suraksha Yojana cash payments for institutional delivery
cases.period: Scheme launched 2005. Evaluation compares district household surveys from 2002-04 and 2007-09.
cases.intervention: The Government of India launched Janani Suraksha Yojana in 2005 as a conditional cash transfer that pays women to give birth in a health facility, with the aim of reducing maternal and neonatal deaths. Receipt of payment varied widely by state, from under 5% to 44% of women giving birth in 2007-08.
cases.verdict_basis: Lim et al. report a significant rise in antenatal care and in-facility births, the behaviours the scheme paid for. The mortality result depends on the method: matching gives 3.7 fewer perinatal deaths per 1000 pregnancies (95% CI 2.2 to 5.2), but a replication using district differences in differences found no significant effect on perinatal or neonatal deaths.
cases.design_detail: Three approaches on district-level household survey data: exact matching of women who did and did not receive JSY payment, a with-versus-without comparison, and district-level differences in differences. The effect is of receiving a payment, compared across women, so selection into payment is a threat.
cases.sample: Lim et al. N as listed in the 3ie replication paper: 182,869 for the logistic regression of payment receipt and 158,907 for the exact matching analysis of in-facility births (births after 1 January 2004), using DLHS-3 (2007-09). Counts taken from a secondary source, not from the Lancet paper itself.

effects.outcome: Antenatal care and births in a health facility
effects.result: Significant increase in both (matching, with-versus-without and differences in differences)
effects.quote: JSY had a significant effect on increasing antenatal care and in-facility births.

effects.outcome: Perinatal deaths, matching analysis
effects.result: Reduction of 3.7 per 1000 pregnancies
effects.quote: JSY payment was associated with a reduction of 3.7 (95% CI 2.2-5.2) perinatal deaths per 1000 pregnancies

effects.outcome: Neonatal deaths, matching analysis
effects.result: Reduction of 2.3 per 1000 livebirths
effects.quote: 2.3 (0.9-3.7) neonatal deaths per 1000 livebirths

effects.outcome: Perinatal and neonatal deaths, with-versus-without comparison
effects.result: Reduction of 4.1 perinatal deaths per 1000 pregnancies and 2.4 neonatal deaths per 1000 livebirths
effects.interval_or_se: Perinatal 95% CI 2.5 to 5.7; neonatal 95% CI 0.7 to 4.1
effects.quote: the reductions were 4.1 (2.5-5.7) perinatal deaths per 1000 pregnancies and 2.4 (0.7-4.1) neonatal deaths per 1000 livebirths

effects.outcome: Perinatal and neonatal deaths, district differences in differences
effects.result: No significant effect on perinatal or neonatal deaths
effects.quote: found no significant effect of JSY on perinatal and neonatal deaths in the district-level differences-indifferences analysis
effects.page_or_section: Replication of Lim et al., district differences-in-differences analysis

effects.outcome: Births in a public health facility, district differences in differences
effects.result: Rise of 19 percentage points, a doubling of the rate, if the scheme were implemented at full coverage; in practice the increase is substantially smaller because implementation was incomplete
effects.quote: when implemented at full coverage, the JSY leads to a 19 percentage point increase or a doubling in the rate of utilisation
effects.page_or_section: Introduction (Powell-Jackson, Mazumdar and Mills, first version, 20 September 2011)

effects.outcome: Neonatal and early neonatal mortality, district differences in differences
effects.result: No statistically significant effect on either
effects.quote: finding no statistically significant effect on either neonatal mortality (deaths within 28 days of birth) or early neonatal mortality (deaths within 24 hours of birth)
effects.page_or_section: Introduction (Powell-Jackson, Mazumdar and Mills, first version, 20 September 2011)

caveats: The evaluation compares districts with different levels of JSY payments in survey data from 2002-04 and 2007-09. It is not a randomised trial, and the mortality effect changes with the method used.
The 3ie replication team reports it replicated the exact matching results closely, but it did not replicate the with-versus-without or differences-in-differences analyses.
The mortality result is not consistent across designs. Matching and with-versus-without show reductions. District differences in differences shows no significant effect, per the 3ie paper.
Matching compares women who received payment with women who did not. Unobserved differences between them could inflate the coverage effect.
The abstract says the poorest and least educated women did not always have the highest odds of receiving payment.
Maternal mortality was assessed but the abstract gives no result for it. See not_verified.

Powell-Jackson and colleagues find the facility-birth effect larger for less educated, poorer and marginalised women, and could not assess maternal mortality for lack of suitable data. Their placebo check found little or no effect on antenatal care, which the scheme did not pay for.
