cases.title: Community participation in village education committees in Jaunpur
cases.period: Interventions September to December 2005; baseline March to April 2005; endline March to April 2006
cases.intervention: Three interventions were tested to raise community involvement in schools through the Village Education Committees (VECs) set up under the Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan. The first gave information about the VEC and the school system at village meetings; the second added training for community members to test children's reading and produce village report cards; the third added volunteers trained to run reading camps of two to three months outside school.
cases.verdict_basis: The first two arms changed neither community involvement nor learning: an increase of 0.12 standard deviations in VEC activism and of 0.06 standard deviations in parental involvement with schools is rejected at the 5 percent level, and reading effects are about 0.4 percentage points. The third arm raised reading, with children 1.7 percentage points more likely to read at least letters and baseline non-readers 7.9 percentage points more likely to read letters. Those gains came from the camps run outside the school, with no rise in involvement in the school itself. This verdict is a judgement call: if the targeted outcome is read as community involvement in schools, the first two arms did not work and the label would change.
cases.design_detail: Villages were randomly assigned within four randomly chosen blocks of Jaunpur district to one of three treatment arms or a control group. Effects come from regressions of endline outcomes on arm indicators and baseline values, with standard errors clustered by village, and an instrumental variables estimate of the effect of attending a reading camp.
cases.sample: 280 villages in Jaunpur district: 65 villages in each of the three arms and 85 control villages. The baseline covered 2,800 households, 316 schools, 1,029 VEC members and 17,533 children aged 7 to 14 tested in reading and maths; 17,419 children were tested at endline.

effects.outcome: VEC activism (complaints made, resources raised)
effects.result: No detectable change; an increase of 0.12 standard deviations is rejected at the 5 percent level
effects.interval_or_se: Joint effect of the three arms -0.030 standard deviations, SE 0.076 (Table 1, Panel B)
effects.quote: Thus, we can reject at the 5 percent level that the intervention increased VEC activism by 0.12 standard deviations.

effects.outcome: Parental involvement with schools (visits, time or money volunteered)
effects.result: No detectable change in any arm; an increase of 0.06 standard deviations is rejected at the 5 percent level
effects.quote: We can reject at the 5 percent level an increase of 0.06 standard deviations in parents’ involvement with the schools for any treatment, which would be a very small effect.

effects.outcome: Parents' knowledge that a VEC exists
effects.result: 2.9 percentage points higher in treatment villages, against 4 percent in the control at endline
effects.quote: Parents in treatment villages are 2.9 percentage points more likely to know that a VEC exists (compared to only 4 percent in the control at endline).

effects.outcome: Child attendance at school
effects.result: No detectable change; an increase of 0.04 standard deviations is ruled out at the 5 percent level
effects.interval_or_se: Joint effect of the three arms -0.094 standard deviations, SE 0.069 (Table 3, Panel B)
effects.quote: We can thus rule out at the 5 percent level a 0.04 standard deviation increase in child presence in school, a small effect.

effects.outcome: School resources and teacher presence
effects.result: No effect found in any arm
effects.quote: Overall, we find no effect on school resources, nonteaching resources or teacher presence (Web Appendix, Table 9).

effects.outcome: Reading among all children, arms 1 and 2
effects.result: No effect on reading or maths; levels in arms 1 and 2 rose as much as in the comparison group
effects.interval_or_se: Share reading at least letters: arm 1 0.004 (SE 0.007), arm 2 0.004 (SE 0.007) (Table 4, Panel A)
effects.quote: Both reading and math levels increased as much in the comparison group as in either treatment 1 or treatment 2.

effects.outcome: Reading among all children in arm 3 villages (reading camps)
effects.result: 1.7 percentage points more likely to read at least letters
effects.interval_or_se: Letters 0.017 (SE 0.007), significant at the 5 percent level; words or paragraphs 0.018 (SE 0.008), also significant at the 5 percent level (Table 4, Panel A)
effects.quote: children in the villages that received intervention 3 are 1.7 percent more likely to read at least letters

effects.outcome: Reading letters among children who could read nothing at baseline, arm 3
effects.result: 7.9 percentage points more likely to read at least letters at endline
effects.quote: Children who could not read anything at the baseline are 7.9 percent more likely to be able to read at least letters at the endline in intervention 3 villages.

effects.outcome: Reading letters among baseline non-readers who attended a reading camp (instrumental variables)
effects.result: 60 percentage points more likely to read letters after attending the camp
effects.interval_or_se: 0.602 (SE 0.304); first stage 0.131 (SE 0.023) (Table 4, Panel B, columns 6 and 7)
effects.quote: A child who could not read at all is 60 percentage points more likely to read letters after attending the reading class.

caveats: Only about 8 percent of children in arm 3 villages attended a reading camp, so village-wide effects are small even though the effect on attendees is large. The attendee estimates assume the whole arm 3 effect works through camp attendance, and they apply to children who chose to attend.
The paper writes some percentage-point differences as percent. The regression tables report them as proportions, for example 0.017 for 1.7.
Arm 2 villages hired 0.23 more Shiksha Mitras (community-hired local teachers) than the control mean of 1.2, significant at the 5 percent level; this is the only school-level gain found.
The results are for one district of Uttar Pradesh and the VEC structure as it stood in 2005 to 2006. Of 88 baseline characteristics, 3 differed significantly between groups.
Quotes and page numbers are taken from the published article as hosted by MIT Economics.

sources.citation: Banerjee, A.V., Banerji, R., Duflo, E., Glennerster, R. and Khemani, S. (2010). Pitfalls of Participatory Programs: Evidence from a Randomized Evaluation in Education in India. American Economic Journal: Economic Policy 2(1): 1-30.
Journal page for the published article, American Economic Journal: Economic Policy 2(1).

cases.title: Aadhaar-based biometric authentication in Jharkhand's ration shops
cases.period: ePOS devices introduced from August 2016; first follow-up January to March 2017; reconciliation of grain disbursals began July 2017 and was paused after four months
cases.intervention: The Government of Jharkhand installed electronic point-of-sale machines in ration shops and required beneficiaries to authenticate by fingerprint against a seeded Aadhaar number to collect Public Distribution System grain. In a second phase it cut each shop's grain allocation by the amount authenticated records showed was undistributed.
cases.verdict_basis: Biometric authentication, the randomised arm, did not reduce leakage, which is what it targeted: the estimate is +Rs 14 per ration card-month (SE 12). It raised beneficiary transaction costs by Rs 6.9 (SE 3.8) and left 2.4 percentage points more households receiving nothing (SE 1.4, p<0.1). The later reconciliation phase was not randomised. It cut leakage and also cut the benefits received.
cases.design_detail: Cluster randomised rollout of ABBA across 132 sub-districts in 10 districts, with reconciliation (launched at the same time in all areas) studied by a pre-specified event study with a placebo commodity group and experimental variation in exposure time. The reconciliation estimates are quasi-experimental.
cases.sample: 132 sub-districts in 10 districts, representative of 15.1 million individuals in 3.3 million households in 17 of 24 districts; panel of 3,840 PDS beneficiaries; administrative data on all 8,924 ration shops in the study area

effects.outcome: Leakage (value disbursed minus value received), per ration card-month, ABBA arm
effects.result: +Rs 14 (control mean Rs 116); 95% CI -1.7% to +6.6% of value disbursed
effects.quote: We estimate that leakage increased insignificantly by Rs. 14 per ration card × month.

effects.outcome: Value disbursed by government, ABBA arm
effects.result: +Rs 12 per ration card-month (about 2%)
effects.quote: a small but significant increase in total value disbursed of Rs. 12 per ration-card month, or around 2%

effects.outcome: Value received by beneficiaries, ABBA arm
effects.result: No significant change in value received
effects.quote: no significant change in overall value received

effects.outcome: Beneficiary transaction costs to collect benefits
effects.result: +Rs 6.9, about Rs 7 on a base of Rs 41 (17%)
effects.quote: beneficiaries did incur 17% higher flow transaction costs to collect their benefits (a Rs. 7 increase on a base of Rs. 41)

effects.outcome: Probability of receiving no commodity in a month
effects.result: +2.4 percentage points (control mean 85% receive any); about 296,000 people denied benefits including non-study districts
effects.quote: The probability that a beneficiary received no commodities at all in a given month increased by an estimated 2.4 percentage points (p < 0.1)

effects.outcome: Households that had not seeded Aadhaar at baseline (23% of households): receiving none of the commodities
effects.result: Probability of receiving nothing rose by 10 percentage points
effects.quote: their probability of receiving none of these commodities increased by 10 percentage points

effects.outcome: Reconciliation phase, first month, control areas: value disbursed
effects.result: Value disbursed fell 19% in the first month
effects.quote: the onset of reconciliation coincided with a sharp 19% drop in value disbursed by the government in control areas

caveats: The cited working paper is the September 2021 revision; the NBER page lists a published version in The Review of Economics and Statistics, and figures there may differ.
The 2.4 point rise in households receiving nothing is significant only at the 10% level.
The authors attribute much of the exclusion to how the transition was managed: no manual override for unseeded households, and dealers held liable for earlier undistributed grain.
The reconciliation results are not from a randomised arm and run only for four months before the state paused the policy.
Leakage here is measured on the quantity margin and may miss overcharging by dealers.
Reconciliation cut leakage in the paper's own accounting, so the verdict applies to authentication alone, which is the randomised arm.

cases.title: Kilkari mobile health messages for pregnant women and new mothers
cases.intervention: Kilkari sends 72 weekly prerecorded voice calls, averaging 77 seconds, to a family's mobile phone from the second trimester of pregnancy until the child is one year old. The calls cover family planning, immunisation, nutrition, infant feeding, pregnancy care and other reproductive, maternal, newborn and child health topics.
cases.verdict_basis: The pre-specified primary outcome, exclusive breastfeeding, did not change: 10.8% in the intervention arm and 10.4% in the control arm (relative risk 1.04, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.23). The secondary outcome, use of modern reversible contraception, was 3.7 percentage points higher (relative risk 1.12, 95% CI 1.03 to 1.21), and sterilisation was 2.0 points lower. Among the other maternal, newborn and child health practices measured, only immunisation at 10 weeks was significantly higher, and the confidence interval for that result starts at 1.00.
cases.design_detail: Individually randomised, parallel, unblinded trial with block randomisation stratified by gestational age, parity, age and phone ownership. Analysis was modified intention to treat with log-binomial regression clustered by village, plus an instrumental variable analysis for women who listened to at least half of the relevant call content. Outcomes were self-reported except immunisation, which also used the child health card. The endline survey took place 12 months after birth.
cases.sample: 5,095 women 4 to 7 months pregnant who could speak Hindi and had access to a mobile phone in four districts of Madhya Pradesh (Rewa, Mandsaur, Rajgarh and Hoshangabad); 2,695 were assigned to receive Kilkari and 2,400 to the control arm. The women's endline analysis covers 4,423 women, and 3,842 of their husbands were also surveyed.

effects.outcome: Exclusive breastfeeding in the first 6 months (primary outcome)
effects.result: Relative risk 1.04 (intention to treat) and 1.10 (instrumental variable); no significant effect
effects.interval_or_se: 95% CI 0.88 to 1.23 (intention to treat); 95% CI 0.67 to 1.81 (instrumental variable)
effects.quote: Kilkari was not observed to have a significant impact on exclusive breast feeding (ITT, RR: 1.04, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.23, p=0.64; IV, RR: 1.10, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.81, p=0.71).
effects.page_or_section: Results, Primary outcome: exclusive breast feeding

effects.outcome: Use of modern reversible contraceptives since the birth (secondary outcome)
effects.result: 3.7% higher use; relative risk 1.12
effects.quote: Kilkari was associated with a 3.7% higher use of modern reversible contraceptives (RR: 1.12, 95% CI 1.03 to 1.21, p=0.007)

effects.outcome: Use of modern reversible contraceptives, women who listened to at least half of the relevant content (instrumental variable)
effects.result: Relative risk 1.72
effects.quote: using both ITT (RR: 1.12, 95% CI 1.03 to 1.21, p=0.007) and IV (RR: 1.72, 95% CI 1.06 to 2.77, p=0.028) analyses
effects.page_or_section: Results, Secondary outcome: modern reversible contraceptive methods

effects.result: 2.0% lower proportion sterilised; relative risk 0.85
effects.quote: a 2.0% lower proportion of men or women sterilised since the birth of the child (RR: 0.85, 95% CI 0.74 to 0.97, p=0.016)

effects.outcome: Children immunised at 10 weeks
effects.result: 2.8% higher in the intervention arm; relative risk 1.04
effects.quote: the proportion of children immunised at 10 weeks was 2.8% higher in the intervention arm as compared with the control arm (ITT, RR: 1.04, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.07, p=0.048)
effects.page_or_section: Results, Effects on other RMNCH practices

effects.outcome: Child fully immunised at 12 months
effects.result: 41.7% intervention against 40.5% control; relative risk 1.02; no significant effect
effects.quote: Child fully immunised at 12 months 41.7 40.5 1.22 1.02 0.95 to 1.10 0.53

effects.outcome: Listening to Kilkari calls (exposure)
effects.result: An average of 65% listened to at least half of the cumulative content of calls answered
effects.quote: An average of 65% of the 2695 women randomised to receive Kilkari listened to ≥50% of the cumulative content of calls answered.

effects.outcome: Share of subscribers who listened to more than 75% of call content
effects.result: 31% listened to more than 75% of the total content of calls
effects.quote: An average of 65% of subscribers listened to more than 50% of the cumulative total of successful calls while 31% listened to more than 75% of the total content of calls.

caveats: 44% of the women changed their SIM card between baseline and endline and stopped receiving calls, which the authors say lowered compliance and statistical power.
Women who kept the same SIM tended to be more educated, richer and from advantaged castes, so the instrumental variable estimates describe listeners who were easier to keep reaching.
All outcomes except immunisation are self-reported at a single point 12 months after birth, so they are open to recall and social desirability bias.
The reversible contraception outcome was added after trial registration, though it appears in the published protocol. The authors treat exclusive breastfeeding as the primary outcome.
The authors report a 12-month exclusive breastfeeding rate of about 10%, far below the 58% in the National Family Health Survey for the state, because they use a stricter two-question definition.

The abstract gives the 10-week immunisation result as relative risk 1.03 (95% CI 1.00 to 1.06) while the results text and table give 1.04 (1.00 to 1.07). The paper also reports lower immediate breastfeeding in the intervention arm with p-values that differ between text and table.

The sample was women with access to a phone during the day, who the authors say are likely more advantaged than pregnant women in general. Many outcomes were tested with no adjustment for multiple comparisons.
Husbands may have listened to some calls, so the contraception effect may partly reflect men's exposure.

cases.title: MGNREGA and rural labour markets: public works, private work and wages
cases.period: Programme phased in from February 2006 (200 districts), April 2007 (130 districts) and April 2008 (rest of rural India); outcomes compared between July 2004 to June 2005 and July 2007 to June 2008
cases.intervention: The National Rural Employment Guarantee Act offers rural households public works employment on demand. The central government introduced it district by district, starting with the poorest districts.
cases.verdict_basis: The guarantee raised public works employment and rural wages, but the effect depends on state implementation. Nationally, public works time rose 1.17 percentage points in the dry season (SE 0.298) and private wages rose 4.7 log points (SE 2.1). In the seven 'star' states public works time rose 3.1 points. The paper reports no rise in public employment in the other states.
cases.design_detail: Difference-in-differences comparing 288 districts that received the programme in the first two phases (early) with 209 districts that received it in 2008 (late), using National Sample Survey employment rounds. Phase assignment was not random: early districts were chosen for low agricultural wages, a larger share of backward castes and low agricultural output per worker.
cases.sample: 497 districts; 356,636 adults aged 18 to 60 in the National Sample Survey sample used for the employment outcomes (Table 3 observations)

effects.outcome: Time spent on public works, dry season, all India (percentage points of total time)
effects.result: +1.17 percentage points (rainy season +0.46)
effects.quote: Public works employment increased by 1.17 percentage points during the dry season and 0.46 percentage points during the rainy season.
effects.page_or_section: Section 5.2 and Table 3, column 1 (accepted manuscript, pp. 17 and 39)

effects.outcome: Time spent on private sector work, dry season
effects.result: -1.306 percentage points (significant at 10 percent only); private work fell 1.46 percent
effects.quote: private sector work declined by 1.31/.893 = 1.46%

effects.outcome: Log deflated daily casual earnings, dry season (private wage)
effects.result: +4.73 log points (about 4.7%)
effects.quote: The estimated 4.7% increase in wages and 1.5% decrease in private employment imply a 0.31 elasticity of labor demand

effects.outcome: Time spent on public works, dry season, seven star states
effects.result: +3.1 percentage points; no rise in other states
effects.quote: time spent on public employment in early districts of star states rises by 3.1 percentage points in the dry season

effects.outcome: Casual wage, dry season, star states
effects.quote: in star states, daily casual earnings increase by a strongly significant 8.98% in the dry season

caveats: Early districts were chosen because they were poorer, so differences between early and late districts may partly reflect different trends.
The authors find a positive pre-programme trend in casual wages in early districts, which disappears once district controls are added.
The employment effects are concentrated in the dry season and in seven states that delivered most of the programme's employment.
The fall in private work is significant only at the 10% level, and unemployment did not fall.
The post period covers at most about two years of programme exposure.

cases.title: Group microcredit in Hyderabad neighbourhoods
cases.period: Spandana opened branches from 2005. Households were surveyed 15 to 18 months later and again two years after that, three to 3.5 years after microfinance arrived.
cases.intervention: The microfinance institution Spandana opened group-lending branches in 52 of 104 poor Hyderabad neighbourhoods chosen at random. It lends to groups of women who are jointly responsible for each loan, and offers no business training.
cases.verdict_basis: Borrowing from microfinance institutions rose by 8.4 percentage points. Investment and profits of businesses that already existed rose, with profits up Rs. 2,206 a month from a control mean of Rs. 2,000, concentrated in the top tail of profitability. Average profits across all households did not rise significantly, consumption did not change, and the index of 16 social outcomes moved by 0.007 standard deviations.
cases.design_detail: Neighbourhood-level randomised trial with intention-to-treat estimates. Other lenders entered treatment and control areas, so the difference in borrowing between the two is modest.
cases.sample: About 6,850 households in 104 neighbourhoods at the first endline, an average of 65 per neighbourhood, re-surveyed two years later.

effects.outcome: Probability a household has a loan from a microfinance institution, first endline
effects.result: 8.4 percentage points higher in treated areas (26.7% versus 18.3%)
effects.quote: the probability of receiving an MFI loan was still 8.4 percentage points (46%) higher in treatment areas than in comparison areas (26.7% borrowers in treated areas versus 18.3% borrowers in comparison areas)

effects.outcome: Spending on business durables over the last year, all households, first endline
effects.result: Rs. 391 more in treated areas, statistically significant
effects.quote: the point estimate is small in absolute value (Rs. 391 over the last year, or a bit less than a third of the increase in average MFI borrowing in treatment households)

effects.outcome: Monthly profit of businesses that existed before microcredit arrived, first endline
effects.result: Rs. 2,206 higher in treated areas against a control mean of Rs. 2,000, concentrated in the top tail of profitability
effects.quote: We find an average increase in profits of Rs. 2,206 in treatment areas, which is statistically significant and represents more than doubling, relative to the control mean of Rs. 2,000.

effects.outcome: Monthly business profit across all households, first endline
effects.result: Rs. 354 per month higher, about a 50% increase on the comparison mean but not statistically significant
effects.quote: The point estimate, at Rs. 354 per month, corresponds to a roughly 50% increase relative to the profits received by the average comparison household.

effects.outcome: Total consumption per adult equivalent, first endline
effects.result: No significant change; the estimate is close to zero
effects.quote: The 90% CIs are (-51, 71) for total consumption and (-59, 46) for non-durable consumption.

effects.outcome: Spending on temptation goods per capita, first endline
effects.result: About Rs. 9 per month lower in treated areas
effects.quote: Spending on temptation goods is reduced by about Rs. 9 per capita per month (column 7).

effects.outcome: Index of 16 social outcomes including women's decision-making, first endline
effects.result: No effect; point estimate .007 standard deviations
effects.quote: Column 7 shows that there is no effect on the index of social outcomes (point estimate .007 standard deviations)

effects.outcome: Business assets and profits after three years, second endline
effects.result: Treated-area businesses had significantly more assets and larger profits above the 85th percentile; no difference in average consumption
effects.quote: businesses in the treatment groups have significantly more assets, and business profits are now larger for businesses above the 85th percentile of profitability

caveats: Take-up was low and the gap in borrowing between treatment and control areas was only 8.4 percentage points, so the estimates reflect marginal borrowers and have limited power.
By the second endline, control areas also had microcredit, so the later comparison is between longer and shorter exposure rather than access against none.
The lender is for-profit, offers no training, and worked in neighbourhoods it was undecided about, in a period of fast economic growth.
Figures come from the March 2014 working paper, which updates and supersedes the 2010 version; it is an author-hosted copy of the paper later published in AEJ: Applied Economics 7(1).

sources.citation: Banerjee, A., Duflo, E., Glennerster, R. and Kinnan, C. (2015). The miracle of microfinance? Evidence from a randomized evaluation. American Economic Journal: Applied Economics 7(1), 22-53. Version read: author-hosted working paper dated March 2014.

cases.title: India's midday meal programme and children's test scores
cases.period: Supreme Court directive 2001; states introduced meals between 2002 and 2006; ASER data 2005-2012
cases.intervention: A 2001 Supreme Court directive required free cooked midday meals in government primary schools. States introduced them at different dates between 2002 and 2006, run by state governments and local bodies.
cases.verdict_basis: About five years of exposure raised reading scores 18% (0.17 SD) and maths scores 9% (0.09 SD) compared with under a year of exposure. The design is quasi-experimental, so the result rests on a parallel-trends assumption that the authors say cannot be tested formally.
cases.design_detail: Difference-in-differences style intent-to-treat design. Staggered state rollout and birth cohort give variation in months of potential exposure; regressions include state, birth-year and survey-year fixed effects and state-specific linear time trends. Identification relies on parallel trends in test scores across early and late implementing states.
cases.sample: ASER household survey, rural India, 8 cross-sections 2005-2012; the main sample of 6 to 10 year olds is 1,238,781 child observations in 24 states and union territories (2016 working paper version).

effects.outcome: Reading score, long exposure (up to five years) versus under one year
effects.quote: increases test scores by 18% (0.17 σ) for reading and 9% (0.09 σ) for math relative to children with less than a year of exposure

effects.outcome: Math score, long exposure versus under one year
effects.quote: increases test scores by 18% (0.17 σ) for reading and 9% (0.09 σ) for math relative to children with less than a year of exposure

effects.outcome: Who benefited
effects.result: no difference by gender or housing assets; gains larger where teaching inputs were present
effects.quote: All children, irrespective of gender or wealth, benefit equally from the program.

effects.outcome: Shape of effect
effects.result: rises over the first three years of exposure, then tapers
effects.quote: the effect of program exposure on test performance is increasing in the first 3 years of exposure and then tapers off

effects.outcome: Cost relative to teaching inputs
effects.result: cost per child almost three times higher than extra teachers or tutoring, so less test-score gain per rupee
effects.quote: this improvement comes at a cost per child that is almost three times higher than these teaching and tutoring inputs

caveats: The main sample is 6 to 10 year olds, the primary school ages. Extending to 5 to 11 year olds was a sensitivity check that, per the IZA draft, did not change results.
There is no pure control group. Every child in the sample had at least 4 months of potential exposure, so the comparison is long versus short exposure, and meals versus none cannot be estimated.
Exposure is intent-to-treat and based on age and state rollout date, not on whether a child ate the meal.
Parallel trends cannot be formally tested. The authors say so.
Data are rural India only, from a survey where nutritional deficiency was common; the authors say the gains may reflect a very disadvantaged population.
Outcomes are ASER reading and arithmetic levels on a 0 to 4 scale, which are basic skills.
The sample size comes from the 2016 working paper version; the journal version may differ.

sources.citation: Chakraborty and Jayaraman (2019), School feeding and learning achievement: Evidence from India's midday meal program, Journal of Development Economics 139:249-265 (abstract, introduction and conclusion snippets on publisher page)
Chakraborty and Jayaraman (2016), School Feeding and Learning Achievement: Evidence from India's Midday Meal Program, IZA Discussion Paper 10086

cases.title: Mission Indradhanush and Intensified Mission Indradhanush vaccination drives
cases.intervention: Mission Indradhanush (from 2015) and Intensified Mission Indradhanush (October 2017 to January 2018) periodically intensified routine immunisation in districts with weak coverage. Health workers first surveyed households door to door to find under-vaccinated children, districts drew up micro-plans for session sites, community workers ran awareness drives, and auxiliary nurse midwives held extra immunisation sessions for seven consecutive days a month.
cases.verdict_basis: In the stronger analysis, the controlled interrupted time-series of Intensified Mission Indradhanush, delivery of 13 infant vaccines rose by a median 10.6% (95% CI 5.1% to 16.5%) during the four months of implementation, and immunisation sessions rose by 11.2%. The authors found no sustained effect in the eight months afterwards, and over the full year the estimated gains in coverage and in unvaccinated children reached were not statistically significant for any vaccine. The earlier survey study of the first two phases of Mission Indradhanush found full immunisation 27% higher and on-time vaccination 8% higher in programme districts, but with a weaker design.
cases.design_detail: Main source: controlled interrupted time-series (comparative interrupted time-series) using monthly district counts of vaccine doses from the Health Management Information System, October 2015 to September 2018, with quasi-Poisson models, district and calendar-month fixed effects, and a four-month implementation period plus two four-month follow-up periods. A second source, the Annals paper, uses difference in difference on household survey data from the Integrated Child Health and Immunization Survey (rounds 1 and 3), comparing districts covered by Mission Indradhanush phases 1 and 2 with uncovered districts.
cases.sample: Health Policy and Planning study: 179 districts that took part in Intensified Mission Indradhanush and 439 that did not, out of 187 and 549 originally. Annals study: 9,674 children under 2 (3,929 in programme districts and 5,745 in other districts) from 48 districts in the survey.

effects.outcome: Doses delivered during the four months of implementation, 13 infant vaccines (median)
effects.result: Median increase of 10.6%
effects.quote: during implementation, IMI increased delivery of 13 infant vaccines, with a median effect of 10.6% (95% confidence interval 5.1% to 16.5%)

effects.outcome: Doses delivered during implementation, first and third doses of DTP-containing vaccine
effects.result: 12.8% for DTP1 and 10.0% for DTP3
effects.interval_or_se: 95% CI 5.3% to 21.0% for DTP1; 4.4% to 15.8% for DTP3
effects.quote: The point estimates for DTP1 and DTP3 were 12.8% (95% CI 5.3 to 21.0) and 10.0% (95% CI 4.4 to 15.8), respectively.

effects.outcome: Immunisation sessions held per treated district during implementation
effects.result: 11.2% increase
effects.quote: IMI was estimated to have increased the number of immunization sessions held per treated district by 11.2% (95% CI 3.7 to 19.4)

effects.outcome: Doses delivered in the eight months after implementation ended (June to September 2018)
effects.result: Median change of 2.7%, none statistically significant
effects.quote: Point estimates for all estimated effects were positive from June to September 2018 (median value 2.7%), with the exception of OPVb, for which the estimated effect was negative, but none of the effects was statistically significant.

effects.outcome: Additional infants reached with each vaccine over the first 12 months
effects.result: 148 000 to 491 000 per vaccine, not statistically significant
effects.interval_or_se: Confidence intervals include a reduction in children reached
effects.quote: None of these estimates were statistically significant. We estimated that IMI reached between 148 000 and 491 000 additional infants with each of the vaccines in the study.

effects.outcome: Share of otherwise unvaccinated children reached, first doses of DTP and polio
effects.result: Approximately one-third
effects.interval_or_se: DTP1: 35.7% reached, 95% CI from -7.5% to 77.4%, not statistically significant
effects.quote: IMI reached approximately one-third of children who would otherwise not have received these vaccines.

effects.outcome: Full immunisation, children under 2 in Mission Indradhanush phase 1 and 2 districts against other districts
effects.result: 27% higher
effects.interval_or_se: Difference-in-difference coefficient 0.27, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.42, from a linear probability model
effects.quote: The full immunization rate was 27% higher among children under 2 years old residing in MI phase 1 and 2 districts (intervention group) as compared with those residing elsewhere (control group).
effects.page_or_section: Abstract (Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences)

effects.outcome: Receiving all vaccines at recommended ages (timeliness)
effects.result: 8% higher
effects.quote: The rate of receiving all vaccines at recommended ages was 8% higher in the intervention group.
effects.page_or_section: Abstract (Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences)

caveats: The two papers study different parts of the programme. The Annals paper covers Mission Indradhanush phases 1 and 2 (April 2015 to January 2016) with survey data. The Health Policy and Planning paper covers the later Intensified Mission Indradhanush (October 2017 to January 2018) with administrative dose counts.

The two papers disagree in strength. The Annals paper finds large significant gains in full immunisation and timeliness, while the Health Policy and Planning paper finds short gains in doses that fade after the drive and coverage gains that are not statistically significant over a year.

The Health Policy and Planning paper is the main source because it uses monthly data from about 618 districts with two years before the drive and a follow-up period, controls for trends and for displacement of doses that would have been given anyway, does not need parallel trends, and gave similar results in eight alternative specifications.

The Annals paper has a weaker design. The survey did not cover the same districts in each round (48 districts in the analysis, 13 programme districts before and 8 after), and programme districts started well behind (full immunisation 55% against 77%). The parallel trends check used a different survey and only DPT3, and 40% and 34% of households in the two rounds showed no vaccination card.

The Annals paper reports its results as a difference-in-difference coefficient, called a percentage difference in the text. It found no significant differences in districts covered by only one of the two phases.

The Health Policy and Planning paper counts doses, not children, so coverage and unvaccinated-children figures rest on population estimates. It did not measure full immunisation or timeliness directly, and it suggests only that a dip in doses after the drive may mean some children were vaccinated earlier.

Health Management Information System data are noisy, which gives wide intervals. The authors found no evidence that the drive changed reporting, and the measles results may be unreliable because of a concurrent change in measles vaccine delivery.
The Health Policy and Planning paper found no meaningful effect on the two vaccines for pregnant women.

sources.citation: Clarke-Deelder E, Suharlim C and others. Impact of campaign-style delivery of routine vaccines: a quasi-experimental evaluation using routine health services data in India. Health Policy and Planning, 2021, 36(4), 454 to 463.

Improving vaccination coverage and timeliness through periodic intensification of routine immunization: evidence from Mission Indradhanush. Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences, 2021, 1502(1), 110 to 120.

cases.title: Improved cookstoves in rural Odisha
cases.period: Stoves built from September 2006 to April 2010, with households followed for four years after the first offers
cases.intervention: Gram Vikas, an NGO, offered subsidised improved mud stoves with a chimney and two pot holes (the ARTI design, about US$12.50 per stove) to households chosen by public lottery in each village. Stove construction came with training on use and maintenance and a paid village promoter.
cases.verdict_basis: The stoves aimed to cut smoke exposure and improve health. Exhaled carbon monoxide among primary cooks fell by 3.1 percent of the control mean over the four years, which is not statistically significant. The only significant fall was 0.53 ppm (7.5 percent) in year 1, and it was gone by year 2. A standardised index of health outcomes moved by 0.008 standard deviations for primary cooks (standard error 0.014), and lung function, birth weight and illness showed no gains. Wood use and fuel costs did not fall, and repairs rose by 2.431 per year.
cases.design_detail: Within each village a public lottery decided the order in which households received stoves, in three waves. Households offered a stove in the first two waves are compared with households still waiting. Standard errors are clustered at the household level and effects are estimated by months since stove construction.
cases.sample: 2,575 households in 44 villages in the western and southern districts of Odisha (then Orissa), followed for four years. About 94 percent of households were found in the first two main surveys and about 81 percent in the last.

effects.outcome: Meals cooked in a week on a good-condition, low-polluting stove (offered versus not offered)
effects.result: The extra meals fell from 3.472 in year 1 to 1.758 by year 3.
effects.interval_or_se: Standard error 0.229 in year 1 and 0.287 in year 3 (Table 3, column 4)
effects.quote: This fell from 3.472 in Year 1 to 1.758 by Year 3.

effects.outcome: Households with an improved stove installed
effects.result: Households offered a stove were 62 percentage points more likely to have the improved stove than the control group.
effects.quote: the treatment group was 62 percentage points more likely to have a GV stove than the control group

effects.outcome: Improved stoves in good condition
effects.result: The offer raised the share of improved stoves in good condition by 36 percentage points over the whole period.
effects.quote: the treatment effect on the proportion of GV improved stoves in good condition is 36 percentage points over the entire period

effects.outcome: Exhaled carbon monoxide of primary cooks, four-year average
effects.result: Carbon monoxide fell by 3.1 percent of the control mean, which is not statistically significant.
effects.interval_or_se: Coefficient -0.230 ppm, standard error 0.196; control mean 7.128 ppm (Table 4, column 1)
effects.quote: In terms of magnitude, it is small, being 3.1 percent of the mean and 3.6 percent of a standard deviation.

effects.outcome: Exhaled carbon monoxide of primary cooks, year 1
effects.result: In year 1 the reduction was 0.53 ppm, or 7.5 percent of the control mean, when stove use was at its highest.
effects.interval_or_se: Coefficient -0.534 ppm, standard error 0.281, significant at the 10 percent level only (Table 4, panel B)
effects.quote: we find a 0.53 ppm reduction (7.5 percent of the control group’s mean) in the CO concentration during Year 1 for primary cooks

effects.outcome: Exhaled carbon monoxide of primary cooks, years 2 to 4
effects.result: The effect fell to 0.173 ppm by the second year, was no longer significant, and was positive and insignificant in years 3 and 4.
effects.quote: the treatment effect for primary cooks falls to −0.173 ppm by the second year of stove ownership and is no longer significant, and is positive and insignificant by Years 3 and 4

effects.outcome: Exhaled carbon monoxide of children
effects.result: Carbon monoxide among children fell slightly, which is not statistically significant.
effects.interval_or_se: Coefficient -0.120 ppm, standard error 0.181; control mean 5.460 ppm (Table 4, column 2)
effects.quote: For children, the overall effect is also negative, but statistically insignificant

effects.outcome: Lung function of women who cook regularly (spirometry)
effects.result: No difference in lung function between treatment and control women.
effects.quote: no difference in lung functioning (as measured by spirometry tests) between women who regularly cook in the treatment and control groups

effects.outcome: Standardised index of health outcomes
effects.result: The index changed by a 0.008 standard deviation fall for primary cooks and a 0.006 rise for children, neither significant.
effects.interval_or_se: Standard error 0.014 for primary cooks and 0.011 for children (Table 6B, panel A)

effects.outcome: Wood used at the last meal (kg)
effects.result: Wood use did not change: the estimate is 0.046 kg.
effects.interval_or_se: Standard error 0.123; control mean 3.373 kg (Table 7, column 1)

effects.outcome: Fuel costs in the last 30 days (rupees)
effects.result: Reported fuel spending rose by 9.482 rupees, which is not statistically significant.
effects.interval_or_se: Standard error 6.697; control mean 333 rupees (Table 7, column 2)

effects.outcome: Repairs made to the stove in the last year
effects.result: Treatment households made 2.431 more repairs per year.
effects.interval_or_se: Standard error 0.506, significant at the 1 percent level; control mean 5.430 (Table 7, column 4)

caveats: Smoke exposure is measured by carbon monoxide in exhaled breath, a proxy for fine particles, not by direct measurement of fine particles.
The stove is at the lower-cost end of improved designs, and the authors note that stove designs have improved since the study began.
The programme was run by a well-regarded NGO with training and a village promoter, so the authors describe it as a better-than-typical rollout.
The finding concerns stoves that households used irregularly and maintained poorly. It does not show what a stove that is well used and maintained would do.
Cited from the published article as hosted by J-PAL.

sources.citation: Hanna, R., Duflo, E. and Greenstone, M. (2016). Up in Smoke: The Influence of Household Behavior on the Long-Run Impact of Improved Cooking Stoves. American Economic Journal: Economic Policy 8(1): 80-114. Published version, as hosted by J-PAL.

cases.title: Rural roads under the Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana
cases.period: Programme launched in 2000; outcomes measured in 2012 and 2013 data, on average four years after road completion.
cases.intervention: The Government of India's PMGSY funded all-weather roads to unconnected villages, with national guidelines that prioritised villages above population thresholds of 1,000 and then 500 (2001 Census). By 2015 it had funded roads to nearly 200,000 villages at a cost of almost 40 billion US dollars.
cases.verdict_basis: Roads raised transport use (index +0.410, SE 0.187) and cut the share of workers in agriculture by 9.2 percentage points (SE 0.043). Predicted consumption (+0.022 log points, SE 0.038), agricultural yields and assets showed no significant change, and village firm employment rose only slightly (index p = 0.09).
cases.design_detail: Fuzzy regression discontinuity. Programme guidelines prioritised villages above population thresholds of 500 and 1,000 (2001 Census), so villages just above a threshold were about 22 percentage points more likely to get a road. Estimates use local linear regression with a triangular kernel, an optimal bandwidth of 84 around the thresholds, district-by-threshold fixed effects and baseline controls.
cases.sample: 11,432 villages that had no paved road in 2001, matched across datasets, and fell within the optimal bandwidth of a population threshold. Household outcomes come from the 2012 Socioeconomic and Caste Census; firm outcomes from the Economic Census.

effects.outcome: Probability of getting a PMGSY road, villages just above vs below the threshold (first stage)
effects.result: About 22 percentage points higher
effects.quote: This rule causes villages just above the population threshold to be 22 percentage points more likely to receive a road

effects.outcome: Share of workers (aged 21 to 60) in agriculture
effects.result: -9.2 percentage points (19 percent below the control mean of 0.476)
effects.quote: New roads cause a 9.2 percentage point reduction in workers in agriculture (representing a 19 percent decrease from the control group mean)

effects.outcome: Employment in village non-farm firms (log, all sectors)
effects.result: 4.2 new jobs per village on average (log change +0.273, not significant at 5 percent)
effects.quote: We estimate that a new road on average creates 4.2 new jobs in a village.

effects.outcome: Predicted consumption per capita
effects.result: +2 percent (+0.022 log points), not significant; the paper rules out a 10 percent increase at 95 percent confidence
effects.quote: We estimate that roads cause a statistically insignificant 2 percent increase in predicted consumption

effects.outcome: Index of agricultural production
effects.result: +0.082, not significant
effects.page_or_section: AER 110(3), Table 3 (columns: transportation, ag occupation, firms, ag production, consumption)

caveats: Outcomes are observed about four years after road completion, so the paper estimates short- to medium-run effects only.
Consumption is predicted from assets and other measures, not measured directly, because the census microdata contain no wage, input or output variables.

The sample is villages near the 500 and 1,000 population thresholds in states that followed the prioritisation rule, including Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Orissa and Rajasthan, so results apply to those villages.
In Table 5 the fall in agricultural occupation is significant at the 5 percent level, but the matching rise in non-agricultural manual labour (SE 0.043 on an estimate of 0.072) is not.
The authors note that remote areas may continue to lack economic opportunities even with better market connections.

sources.citation: Asher and Novosad (2020), Rural Roads and Local Economic Development, American Economic Review 110(3), 797-823
Asher and Novosad (2020), AER 110(3), publisher abstract page (DOI 10.1257/aer.20180268)

cases.title: Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY and hospital use, out-of-pocket spending and catastrophic spending in six states
cases.period: Household survey in December 2019 to February 2020, about a year after the scheme launched in September 2018
cases.intervention: Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PM-JAY) is a publicly funded national health insurance scheme for economically and socially disadvantaged households. It covers up to Rs 500,000 per family per year for secondary and tertiary hospitalisation in public and empanelled private hospitals.
cases.verdict_basis: Enrolment in PM-JAY was not associated with more hospitalisations. It was associated with a Rs 1,656 (13%) lower out-of-pocket spend per hospitalisation, significant at the 10% level, and an 8 percentage point (21%) lower chance of catastrophic spending, significant at the 1% level. The reductions came entirely from private hospitals, and enrolled people were 4.6 percentage points more likely to be treated in a private rather than a public facility. The authors state that they cannot establish causal impact.
cases.design_detail: Cross-sectional household survey analysed with logistic and ordinary least squares regression, comparing PM-JAY enrolled and non-enrolled eligible individuals while controlling for age, sex, education, caste, wealth quintile, state and other characteristics. Standard errors are clustered at the household level.
cases.sample: 53,486 PM-JAY eligible individuals in 11,618 households for the hospitalisation analysis. 4,047 individuals in 3,411 households with a hospitalisation in the prior 12 months for the spending analysis. Districts within six purposively selected states.

effects.outcome: Probability of hospitalisation in the last 12 months
effects.result: No significant change in hospitalisations among enrolled eligible individuals
effects.quote: PM-JAY was not associated with an increase in hospitalizations

effects.outcome: Use of a private rather than public facility among those hospitalised
effects.result: 4.6 percentage points higher probability of a private facility
effects.quote: It increases the probability of visiting a private facility by 4.6 percentage points at the 5% significance level

effects.outcome: Out-of-pocket expenditure per hospitalisation
effects.result: Rs 1,656 lower, a relative decrease of 13%
effects.quote: the amount of OOPE is reduced by Rs 1,656 at the 10% significance level, which is a relative decrease of 13%

effects.outcome: Out-of-pocket expenditure per hospitalisation in private facilities
effects.result: Rs 2,574 lower, a relative decrease of 17%
effects.quote: The amount of OOPE is reduced by Rs 2,574 at the 10% significance level, which is a relative decrease of 17%

effects.outcome: Out-of-pocket expenditure per hospitalisation in public facilities
effects.result: No significant change in public facilities
effects.quote: For public facilities, we find PM-JAY is not associated with any change in OOPE

effects.outcome: Catastrophic health expenditure (out-of-pocket above 10% of household consumption)
effects.result: 8 percentage points lower chance of catastrophic expenditure, a relative decrease of 21%
effects.quote: PM-JAY is associated with an 8 percentage points reduction in CHE, translating to a relative decrease of 21%

effects.outcome: Catastrophic health expenditure in private facilities
effects.result: 8.5 percentage points lower, a relative decrease of 19%
effects.quote: for private facilities, CHE is reduced by 8.5 percentage points, translating to a relative decrease of 19%

caveats: The authors write that they are unable to examine the causal impacts of the scheme because of the quick national rollout and the resulting study design, so the results are associations.
The six states were purposively selected and the authors say the results cannot be claimed as nationally representative.
Data collection was restricted to rural and semi-urban areas because many households on the eligibility list could not be located.
The data are self-reported and may suffer from recall bias, and the spending result for all facilities is significant only at the 10% level.

sources.citation: Parmar D, Strupat C, Srivastava S, Brenner S, Parisi D, Ziegler S, Neogi R, Walsh C, De Allegri M. Effects of the Indian National Health Insurance Scheme (PM-JAY) on Hospitalizations, Out-of-pocket Expenditures and Catastrophic Expenditures. Health Systems & Reform 2023;9(1):2227430.

cases.title: Rajasthan police reform trials
cases.period: Baseline survey spring 2007, endline survey autumn 2008
cases.intervention: Rajasthan Police tested four reforms recommended by police reform panels in a randomised trial: a freeze on arbitrary transfers, rotation of duties with a weekly day off, a community observer at the station, and on-duty training. A fifth intervention added later was decoy visits, in which field officers posing as crime victims tried to register a case.
cases.verdict_basis: Training raised crime-victim satisfaction with the police by 0.156 to 0.193 on a 0 to 1 scale (significant at 5%) and raised case registration and politeness in decoy visits only in the specification with police station fixed effects (0.233 and 0.196, significant at 5%). The transfer freeze raised victim satisfaction in one specification (0.281) and the lack-of-fear index (0.132 to 0.242). The community observer and the weekly off and duty rotation arms showed no gain, and the observers were present in only 10.29% of designated hours. Public perceptions of corruption did not move with training (0.01 and 0.016).
cases.design_detail: Police stations were randomly assigned, stratified by district, 2005 case load and urban or rural location, to combinations of the reforms. Within stations the share of staff trained was randomised at 0, 25, 50, 75 or 100 percent, and 12 pure control stations were kept outside the study to check for Hawthorne effects. The order of decoy visits was randomised. Outcomes come from a household victimisation survey, a public opinion survey and the decoy visits, analysed with endline-only regressions and with police station fixed effects, standard errors clustered by station.
cases.sample: 162 police stations in 11 districts, over 20% of the state's stations, serving almost 8 million people. Table 6 uses 269 victim reports in the endline-only specification and 571 with station fixed effects; the decoy regressions use 788 visits.

effects.outcome: Crime victim satisfied with police handling of case, per move from no staff trained to all staff trained
effects.result: +0.156 (endline only), +0.193 and +0.131 (police station fixed effects)
effects.interval_or_se: SE 0.0767, 0.0843 and 0.0763; control mean 0.246 (endline) and 0.299 (station fixed effects)
effects.quote: Percentage staff 0.156** 0.193** 0.131*

effects.outcome: Decoy's case registered by police, per move from no staff trained to all staff trained
effects.result: +0.107 and +0.108 (not significant), +0.233 with police station fixed effects (significant at 5%)
effects.interval_or_se: SE 0.0829, 0.0837 and 0.116; control mean at first decoy visit 0.480

effects.outcome: Police very polite to decoy, per move from no staff trained to all staff trained
effects.result: +0.105 and +0.101 (10% level), +0.196 with police station fixed effects (5% level)

effects.outcome: Decoy's case registered, per previous decoy visit to the station (fifth intervention, run by the research team)
effects.result: +0.174, +0.173 and +0.165 per previous decoy visit

effects.outcome: Share of police staff transferred, transfer freeze stations against control
effects.result: 21.1% of staff transferred in freeze stations against 32.8% in control stations, a gap of 11.7 percentage points
effects.interval_or_se: SE 3.59 percentage points, clustered by station

cases.title: Rashtriya Swasthya Bima Yojana and out-of-pocket health spending
cases.period: Scheme launched April 2008. Outcomes measured to March 2012, using survey rounds of 1999-2000, 2004-05 and 2011-12.
cases.intervention: RSBY is a Government of India health insurance scheme launched in April 2008 by the Ministry of Labour and Employment. It covers inpatient care for households on the Below Poverty Line list, with a cover limit of INR 30,000 per family.
cases.verdict_basis: The scheme aimed to lower out-of-pocket health spending. The authors find no significant effect on inpatient out-of-pocket spending or on catastrophic inpatient spending (the 26% fall in early districts was not significant). The probability of any out-of-pocket spending rose by 30% in early districts.
cases.design_detail: Difference in differences with propensity score matching of districts, using the staggered district roll-out. Treated households are the two poorest expenditure quintiles in RSBY districts, a proxy for BPL status. Two treatment groups: districts enrolling by March 2010 (treat1) and between April 2010 and March 2012 (treat2). Estimates are intention to treat.
cases.sample: N = 346,615 households across three NSSO survey rounds, plus district-level RSBY enrolment data (as stated in the abstract). 65,458 households in four excluded states were dropped before analysis, about 18% of the total.

effects.outcome: Inpatient out-of-pocket spending (probability and level)
effects.result: No significant effect
effects.interval_or_se: Standard errors reported in Table 4; not extracted
effects.quote: RSBY did not affect the likelihood of inpatient out-of-pocket spending, the level of inpatient out of pocket spending or catastrophic inpatient spending.

effects.outcome: Catastrophic inpatient spending (OOP above 10% of household consumption expenditure), early districts (treat1)
effects.result: Odds of catastrophic inpatient OOP lower by 26%, not statistically significant
effects.quote: RSBY lowers the likelihood of experiencing catastrophic inpatient OOP spending by 26%, the effect is not statistically significant.

effects.outcome: Catastrophic inpatient spending, later districts (treat2)
effects.result: Lower by almost 9%, not statistically significant
effects.quote: RSBY also lowered the probability of incurring any catastrophic inpatient OOP by almost 9% in ‘treat2’ households, but this was statistically insignificant.

effects.outcome: Probability of any out-of-pocket spending (inpatient and outpatient), early districts
effects.result: Increase of 30%, statistically significant
effects.interval_or_se: Marked significant at the 10 percent level in Table 4
effects.quote: the likelihood of incurring any out of pocket spending (inpatient and outpatient) rose by 30% due to RSBY and was statistically significant.

effects.outcome: Outpatient out-of-pocket spending (level and probability)
effects.result: No statistically significant effect (abstract)
effects.quote: We also do not find any statistically significant effect of RSBY on the level of outpatient out-of-pocket expenditure and the probability of incurring outpatient expenditure.
effects.page_or_section: Abstract. Note: the abstract and Section 4.2.2 differ on the outpatient probability, see caveats.

effects.outcome: Household non-medical spending, early districts
effects.result: Increase of about 5%
effects.quote: RSBY raised household non-medical spending by 5%.

caveats: Estimates are intention to treat for eligible households, not for enrolled households, because the survey cannot identify RSBY status at household level.
Eligibility is proxied by the two poorest expenditure quintiles, which may misclassify some poor households and weaken estimates.

The abstract states no significant effect on the probability of outpatient spending, while Section 4.2.2 reports a significant 23% rise in early districts. The text is internally inconsistent on this point.
Enrolment was under 50% of eligible households in many districts and the authors find no larger effect in high-enrolment districts.
Catastrophic spending is defined only as OOP above 10% of consumption expenditure. Debt and asset sales are not measured.
Authors suggest explanations such as hospital refusals, the INR 30,000 cap and purchases of drugs outside the scheme. These are plausible explanations and are not tested in the paper.

cases.title: Surat particulate matter emissions trading market
cases.period: September 2019 to April 2021, with an interruption caused by the nationwide COVID-19 lockdown.
cases.intervention: The Gujarat Pollution Control Board, working with the research team, built the world's first particulate matter emissions market for coal-burning industrial plants in Surat. Plants assigned to the market received tradeable permits against a cap, with 80 percent of permits given free and 20 percent auctioned weekly, while control plants stayed under standard command-and-control rules.
cases.verdict_basis: Plants in the market cut particulate emissions by a statistically significant amount: -0.193 log points (SE 0.076) without imputed data and -0.282 to -0.316 log points with imputed data, which the authors summarise as a 20 to 30 percent reduction. Compliance with permit obligations was 99 percent against 66 percent under the status quo.
cases.design_detail: Plant-level randomised controlled trial, registered as AEARCTR-0003860. Half of an initial sample of 342 high-pollution-potential plants under the Surat regional office were randomly assigned to the market. All sample plants were required to install continuous emissions monitoring systems. After assignment and before the market began, plants that were closed or seasonal were removed as ineligible.
cases.sample: 162 treatment plants and 156 control plants (318 in total) after ineligible plants were removed, from an initial sample of 342 plants.

effects.outcome: Particulate matter emissions, treatment versus control plants
effects.result: 20 to 30 percent reduction (log-point estimates from -0.178 to -0.316 across specifications)
effects.interval_or_se: Without imputation -0.193 log points, SE 0.076; imputation rule A -0.282, SE 0.074; imputation rule B -0.316, SE 0.057
effects.quote: Second, treatment plants reduced pollution emissions, relative to control plants, by 20%-30%.
effects.page_or_section: QJE 140(2), abstract; Table III and Section IV

effects.outcome: Compliance with the pollution obligation
effects.result: Treatment plants held enough permits to cover emissions 99% of the time, against 66% compliance with standards under the status quo
effects.quote: treatment plants held enough permits to cover their emissions 99% of the time, compared with just 66% compliance with standards

effects.outcome: Variable abatement costs at constant emissions
effects.result: 11 percent lower under the market than under command-and-control (estimated, model-based)
effects.quote: the market reduced abatement costs by an estimated 11%, holding constant emissions
effects.page_or_section: QJE 140(2), abstract; Section on abatement costs

effects.outcome: Benefit-cost comparison of extending the market (mortality benefits against costs)
effects.result: Benefits exceed costs by at least 25 times
effects.quote: the emissions market has mortality benefits that exceed its costs by at least 25 times

effects.outcome: Market design: permit allocation
effects.result: Permits summing to 80% of the cap were distributed free in proportion to emissions potential and 20% were sold in weekly auctions
effects.quote: permits summing to 80% of the cap distributed for free, in proportion to plant emissions potential, and 20% sold off in weekly

caveats: The 20 to 30 percent range depends on how missing emissions readings are handled; the log-point estimates without imputation (about -0.18 to -0.19) convert to roughly 16 to 18 percent by my own arithmetic, so the lower end of the range rests on the imputed specifications.

The paper says the lower emissions in treatment plants came partly from a cap that proved stricter than the control regulation and from the regulator cutting the cap over the first compliance periods.
The cost saving is an estimate from a model of plant bidding, not a direct measurement of spending.
The benefit-cost ratio is for a hypothetical extension of the market across Surat, under assumptions about mortality damages.
The trial covers coal-burning plants in one city and was interrupted by the COVID-19 lockdown.
A research summary from the University of Chicago gives 317 plants; the journal paper gives 318 (162 plus 156), which this page uses.

Converting the log-point estimates (one minus e to the power of the estimate) gives a reduction of about 18 percent without imputed data and about 25 to 27 percent with it, so the lower end of the authors' 20 to 30 percent range depends on the imputation.

cases.title: Total Sanitation Campaign in rural Madhya Pradesh
cases.period: Baseline May to July 2009. Follow-up February to April 2011, 21 months later. The national TSC began in 1999.
cases.intervention: India's Total Sanitation Campaign subsidises and promotes individual household latrines and uses social mobilisation to end open defecation. In Madhya Pradesh it ran with capacity building from the World Bank's Water and Sanitation Program and alongside Nirmal Vatika, which together gave at least Rs 4,200 to below-poverty-line households.
cases.verdict_basis: Latrine coverage rose 19 percentage points (95% CI 12 to 26) and adult open defecation fell about 10 points (95% CI 4 to 15). Diarrhoea (7.4% against 7.7%, p=0.687), gastrointestinal illness, parasites, anaemia and growth showed no difference. Behaviour changed modestly and the child health goal was not met.
cases.design_detail: Cluster randomised controlled trial, randomised at village level with equal allocation to intervention and control. Control villages were promised the programme after the study. Analysis by intention to treat.
cases.sample: 80 rural villages in two districts. Baseline: 3,390 children under 5 from 1,954 households. Follow-up: 5,209 children under 5 from 3,039 households, each with at least one child under 24 months at enrolment. Stool testing on a random subsample of 1,150 children under 24 months.

effects.quote: The intervention increased the coverage of JMP defined improved sanitation facility by average 19 percentage points (95% CI 12%–26%; p-value<0.001)
effects.page_or_section: Results, IHL Coverage and Sanitation-Related Behaviors

effects.outcome: Households with any individual household latrine
effects.result: +20 percentage points (44.1% intervention vs 24.2% control)
effects.quote: The intervention increased the coverage of any type of IHL facility by 20 percentage points (95% CI 13%–27%; p-value<0.001)
effects.page_or_section: Results, IHL Coverage and Sanitation-Related Behaviors

effects.outcome: Daily open defecation, adult women
effects.result: 73% intervention vs 83% control, difference about 10 percentage points
effects.interval_or_se: p<0.001 (abstract gives adult CI 4 to 15 for the pooled adult measure)
effects.quote: adult women (73% intervention versus 83% control; mean difference: 10%; p-value<0.001)
effects.page_or_section: Results, IHL Coverage and Sanitation-Related Behaviors

effects.outcome: Daily open defecation, adult men
effects.result: 75% intervention vs 84% control, difference 9.5 points
effects.quote: adult men (75% intervention versus 84% control; mean difference: 9.5%; p-value = 0.001)
effects.page_or_section: Results, IHL Coverage and Sanitation-Related Behaviors

effects.outcome: Caregiver-reported diarrhoea
effects.result: 7.4% intervention vs 7.7% control, no difference
effects.quote: Diarrhea prevalence did not differ between groups (7.4% intervention versus 7.7% control; p-value = 0.687)

effects.outcome: Highly credible gastrointestinal illness
effects.result: 11.5% intervention vs 12.0% control, no difference
effects.quote: HCGI prevalence also did not differ between groups (11.5% intervention versus 12.0% control; p-value = 0.692)

effects.outcome: Child growth and anaemia
effects.result: No difference between groups
effects.quote: we found no differences between the randomized groups in anemia prevalence or growth outcomes.

caveats: Follow-up was short, 21 months after baseline.
Ten of the 40 control villages were contaminated: TSC activities began in eight control villages soon after baseline and possibly in two more before follow-up.
Diarrhoea, gastrointestinal illness and open defecation are self-reported by caregivers or households, so reporting bias is possible.
Baseline imbalances existed on improved water access (89% vs 80%), handwashing station with soap and water (44% vs 54%), anaemia (88% vs 93%) and height-for-age z-score (-1.38 vs -1.81).
Among households with an improved facility, 41% in intervention villages still reported daily open defecation by adult men or women, against 28% in control villages.
The abstract gives the control mean for adult open defecation as 84%, while the results text gives 83% for women and 84% for men. The pooled adult figure was not separately read.
The authors note the study was funded by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation through the World Bank's Water and Sanitation Program, and one author was World Bank staff.

cases.title: Vajpayee Arogyashree insurance for tertiary care in northern Karnataka
cases.period: Scheme in the northern districts from February 2010, extended statewide in August 2012; household surveys in September 2012
cases.intervention: The Vajpayee Arogyashree scheme gave households with a below poverty line card free tertiary care at empanelled public and private hospitals, with no premium or co-payment. It covered more than 400 service packages, mostly cardiac, cancer, neurological, burn and trauma care, and hospitals ran rural health camps to find patients.
cases.verdict_basis: Among households below the poverty line, mortality from conditions covered by the scheme was 0.32% in eligible villages against 0.90% in ineligible villages, a difference of 0.58 percentage points (95% CI 0.40 to 0.75). Out-of-pocket spending on covered admissions was 34% lower across all facilities and 64% lower for longer tertiary admissions. The rise in use of covered services was not statistically significant (44.2% for longer stays, 95% CI -5.1% to 90.5%). Households above the poverty line, who were ineligible, showed no mortality difference.
cases.design_detail: Geographic regression discontinuity study. Villages just north of the eligibility border (covered from 2010) were compared with propensity score matched villages just south of it (covered only from August 2012), using a one-off household survey in September 2012. Ordinary least squares and logit models with standard errors clustered by village; the author-reported placebo check is households above the poverty line, who were ineligible on both sides.
cases.sample: 31,476 households (22,796 below poverty line) in 300 eligible villages and 28,633 households (21,767 below poverty line) in 272 ineligible villages, in six districts of Karnataka. A detailed spending survey covered 966 below-poverty-line households with covered conditions.

effects.quote: the mortality rate from conditions covered by the scheme was 0.32% in eligible households compared with 0.90% in ineligible households (difference of 0.58 percentage points, 95% confidence interval 0.40 to 0.75

effects.outcome: Mortality from covered conditions, households above the poverty line (ineligible, placebo group)
effects.result: 0.56% in treatment areas against 0.55% in control areas, no difference
effects.quote: 0.56% in treatment areas compared with 0.55% in control areas (difference of 0.01 percentage points, −0.03 to 0.03)

effects.outcome: Out-of-pocket spending on admissions for covered conditions, all facilities
effects.result: 34% reduction in out-of-pocket health expenditure
effects.quote: the scheme was associated with a 34% reduction in out-of-pocket health expenditures for admission to hospital for covered conditions (95% confidence interval 18% to 51%)

effects.outcome: Out-of-pocket spending on covered admissions to tertiary facilities, excluding emergency-only admissions and stays of four days or less
effects.result: 64% reduction in out-of-pocket spending
effects.quote: and to 64% after we excluded short admissions and admissions through the emergency room (35% to 97%)

effects.outcome: Admissions to tertiary facilities for covered conditions with stays longer than four days
effects.result: 44.2% higher use in eligible areas, not statistically significant
effects.quote: non-emergency admissions for potentially covered conditions to tertiary care facilities that led to inpatient stays longer than four days (44.2% difference, −5.1% to 90.5%; P=0.06)
effects.page_or_section: Results, Utilization and foregone medical care; Table 4

effects.result: 35.5% reduction, not statistically significant
effects.quote: (35.5% reduction, 95% confidence interval −73.5% to 2.5%; P=0.07)
effects.page_or_section: Results, Utilization and foregone medical care; Table 4

caveats: Villages were not randomly assigned; the northern districts were chosen for coverage because the state government judged them to be in greater need of tertiary care.
Causes of death are reported by family members, so misclassification is possible, although the authors report sensitivity checks that found no sign of measurement error affecting the results.
The authors could not observe who was actually covered, only whether an admission or death was for a condition the scheme could cover, which they say dilutes the estimates.
Use of covered services is estimated imprecisely, and the authors note the mortality effect could partly reflect previously unmet demand for tertiary care.

cases.title: Reserving panchayat head positions for women
cases.period: Reservation rules applied from 1995 (Rajasthan) and 1998 (West Bengal); the paper reports data collected in 2000 in Birbhum (West Bengal) and Udaipur (Rajasthan) districts.
cases.intervention: Under the 73rd Amendment, one third of Gram Panchayat head (Pradhan) positions were reserved for women, and the councils to be reserved were chosen by a randomised rotation rule. The state governments of West Bengal and Rajasthan implemented the rule; the researchers surveyed the councils afterwards.
cases.verdict_basis: Reserved councils built more drinking water facilities in both states (West Bengal +9.09, SE 4.02; Rajasthan +2.62, SE 0.95). Roads were in better condition in West Bengal (+0.18, SE 0.06) and worse in Rajasthan (-0.08, SE 0.04). Informal education centres fell in West Bengal (-0.16, SE 0.07, council level).
cases.design_detail: Natural randomised policy experiment. In West Bengal, Gram Panchayats in each district were ranked by serial number and every third one was reserved for a woman Pradhan, which makes the reservation as good as random. In Rajasthan a random rotation system was used. Reserved and unreserved councils are compared, and census 1991 village variables show no significant differences between the two groups.
cases.sample: 265 Village Councils (Gram Panchayats) in West Bengal and Rajasthan, per the abstract. West Bengal: all 161 Gram Panchayats of Birbhum district in the study (166 in the district, 5 held back for pre-testing); 322 village-level observations in Table V. Rajasthan: 100 village-level observations in Table V.

The evidence comes from one district per state (Birbhum and Udaipur), surveyed in 2000.
Rajasthan and West Bengal differ in institutions: Rajasthan held its first Panchayat election only in 1995, so the setting has a much shorter history of elected councils.
Reservation changes who leads and also the political competition; the paper argues the results come mainly from the leader's gender.
The paper measures investment in public goods, not the quality, cost or final welfare gains of those goods.
The text of the paper gives the West Bengal village-level count as 322 in Table V and as 323 in a later table note.

cases.title: Women police stations and reported crimes against women
cases.period: 2005 to 2013 (city panel); 1988 to 2013 (state panel)
cases.intervention: Several Indian states created women police stations, staffed by female officers who handle crimes against women and usually led by a woman. Stations opened at different dates across cities and states.
cases.verdict_basis: Reported crimes against women rose by 29.3 percent after a women police station opened in a city, mostly domestic violence (33.5 percent). The authors conclude this reflects more reporting and not more violence: murders linked to love affairs (-0.000), survey-reported intimate-partner violence (-0.042) and reports of non-gendered crime did not rise. Arrest rates for crimes against women overall (-0.078) and for rape (-0.051) and the chargesheet rate (-0.019) did not change, though the arrest rate for female kidnapping rose (0.145).
cases.design_detail: Difference-in-differences exploiting the staggered opening of women police stations. The city analysis uses city and year fixed effects, controls, and event-study plots to check for pre-trends. The state analysis uses state legislation on the stations, and survey outcomes use a triple-difference by treated state, post period and urban residence. Standard errors are clustered by city or state.
cases.sample: City panel of 76 cities, 63 of them treated, for 2005 to 2013 (577 city-years in the main table); state panel of 19 states, 16 of them treated, for 1988 to 2013; Demographic and Health Survey waves of 2005-2006 and 2015-2016 (88,829 women in the violence regression).

effects.quote: enactment of WPS policy leads to an increase in reported GBV of 23.6 percent.

effects.result: No significant change: log coefficients 0.125 and 0.078

effects.result: No significant change: log coefficients 0.325 and -0.000

effects.result: Log coefficient 0.545 without city trends (1% level) and 0.493 with them (not significant)

effects.result: Log coefficient 0.579 (1% level) and 0.283 with city trends (5% level)

effects.result: No change: -0.000 and -0.001

caveats: A rise in recorded crime can reflect more reporting, more police capacity or more crime. The authors conclude the evidence points to more reporting, using murders, a household survey and reports to general police stations as checks on incidence.

Opening dates were not randomly assigned. The authors argue timing was idiosyncratic and test it with placement regressions and event-study plots; staggered difference-in-differences estimates can be biased, and the authors report that 31.1 percent of the weights in the city sample are negative.
Survey and arrest outcomes are available only at state level and rest on two Demographic and Health Survey waves a decade apart.
The station-level check on reports uses Rajasthan only, for January 2006 to December 2007.
The figures and quotes come from the IZA Discussion Paper 14250 version of April 2021; no journal version was found.
